articles.title: Turkey warns Washington against renewed strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Turkey warns Washington against renewed strikes on Iran
TEHRAN– Turkey has warned the United States against launching fresh military strikes on Iran, saying a new attack would widen the conflict across West Asia and that diplomacy remains the only viable path toward ending the war.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan delivered the message on October 23 after meeting with his counterparts from Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in Istanbul. He said the eight countries shared the view that renewed military action against Iran would further destabilize the region.
“We are all in agreement that a new attack on Iran would expand the war in the region,” Fidan said at a joint press conference.
“A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment,” he added, stressing that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to bring the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran to an end.
The meeting brought together foreign ministers from the so-called Regional Four (R4) and the European Union’s E3, alongside Italy, in the first collective gathering of the group in this format.
Discussions focused on the war involving Iran, the risk of further regional escalation, attacks on Saudi Arabia attributed to Yemen’s Ansarallah movement, and the conflict in Ukraine.
The meeting came amid growing reports that Washington was considering renewed military action against Iran following the November 3 US midterm elections, raising concerns among regional and European governments about the prospect of a wider confrontation.
European powers call for de-escalation
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also underscored the need for a diplomatic solution, saying the conflict had continued for too long and imposed an excessive burden on the British public.
 
“The very clear message” is that “diplomacy, dialogue and de-escalation has to be the answer to this conflict,” Miliband told broadcaster ITN. “Frankly, this conflict has gone on too long, the British people have suffered too much from it and we cannot afford months more of it.”
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot warned that further escalation would leave all sides worse off and push oil prices higher, highlighting the potential consequences of a prolonged conflict for global energy markets.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany, France and Britain were prepared to engage in talks with Tehran to address concerns over Iran’s nuclear program.
The statements reflect mounting concern among European governments that renewed hostilities could deepen instability across West Asia, disrupt energy supplies and carry significant economic consequences beyond the region.
The diplomatic push came after The New York Times reported on October 21 that US and Israeli military officials had drawn up detailed plans for renewed strikes against Iran following the US midterm elections.
Citing US officials, the newspaper reported that potential targets could include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone capabilities.
The report intensified concerns over the possibility of another military campaign against Iran and the risk that attacks on critical infrastructure could trigger a broader cycle of retaliation.
Iranian media citing officials that a possible Iranian response to renewed US-Israeli attacks could extend beyond conventional military targets to include undersea cables, data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure in West Asia owned wholly or partly by US investors and commercial interests.
Such scenarios underscore the potential for a wider conflict to affect critical digital infrastructure and economic assets, alongside its more immediate military and energy consequences.
According to Reuters, Fidan said the Istanbul meeting had also addressed possible parameters for preventing the conflict from spreading further, although he did not disclose details of the discussions.

articles.title: How long will Turkey keep its troops in Syria and Iraq?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How long will Turkey keep its troops in Syria and Iraq?
Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler has clarified that Turkey will retain its military presence in Iraq and Syria until certain conditions are met.
The original justifications for Turkey’s cross-border deployments have dwindled in recent years. Now, analysts believe Ankara is offering new justifications for its open-ended military presence in these neighbouring states.
“We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria,” Guler said in a recent interview.
“When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered.”
Open-ended conditions
Turkey sent troops into Syria in 2016. Its cross-border operations primarily focused on targeting the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
The SDF were a coalition formed by the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK)’s main Syria affiliate, which became an invaluable ad hoc US ally against Islamic State (IS).
Early this year, following a Turkish-backed offensive by the new Syrian government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa, the SDF agreed to integrate its fighters into the new Syrian military.
Complete SDF integration could remove Turkey’s decade-long justification for retaining troops in much of northern Syria.
“Ankara conditions its decision to withdraw from Syria not only on border security and the elimination of the terrorist threat in Syria, but also on the al-Sharaa government’s ability to establish state authority throughout the country,” Suleyman Ozeren, a lecturer at the American University and senior fellow at the Orion Policy Institute, told The New Arab.
“This condition could signal Ankara’s desire to maintain a Turkish military presence and use it as leverage against, for example, Israel if tensions in southern Syria escalate into military confrontation between Syria and Israel.”
Consequently, Turkey’s military presence in Syria may continue even if there is a successful Kurdish peace process in Turkey.
“There may be mainly two minimal conditions: the total and actual disarmament of the PKK-linked groups in both Iraq and Syria, and the absence of Israeli military pressure on Syria,” Ozeren said.
In Iraq, Turkey has made repeated forays into northern Iraq’s Nineveh province and Iraqi Kurdistan as part of the conflict with the PKK. Turkey has had bases in these areas since the 1990s.
In the second half of the 2010s, it advanced deeper into the mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, establishing and maintaining a vast network of outposts and forward-operating bases in strategic areas to relentlessly pressure the Kurdish fighters.
Now, with a major peace effort underway aimed at having the PKK lay down its arms for amnesties and a conclusive end to the conflict possibly on the horizon, Turkey’s justifications for these bases could become defunct.
Muaz Al-Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict-tracking organisation Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), specified that Guler’s remarks aren’t a withdrawal signal.
Rather, he was merely articulating the “latest version of an open-ended condition” which Ankara adjusts as events change.
“In 2024, Turkey tied any exit from Syria to a new constitution, elections and full border security. Earlier this year it said the Damascus-SDF deal was still not enough,” Abdullah told The New Arab.
“Withdrawal is possible, because the presence is costly for Turkey economically and politically, but it will be slow and conditional.”
He also outlined how the minimum conditions for withdrawal differ by country.
“In Iraq, the PKK must be disarmed and out of Sinjar and Qandil,” Abdullah said.
“Since the (Turkey-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia) Mecca alliance, Ankara’s concerns now also include the weapons of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and the threat they pose to Turkey’s ally Saudi Arabia, including PMF drone attacks on the Kingdom,” he added.
“In Syria, the minimum is a completed SDF integration, PKK cadres out of the northeast, and a Syrian army able to hold the border on its own.”
Reality on the ground
ACLED data has documented a rapid decrease in Turkish strikes in Iraqi Kurdistan in the past two years since the latest PKK peace talks began. In 2024, Turkey executed 4,861 strikes in the region. That fell rapidly to 634 in 2025, then to zero so far in 2026.
“The security case for staying is weakening, but the political conditions are not yet met,” Abdullah said.
In September, Turkey agreed to gradually withdraw from the Bashiqa base in Nineveh in tandem with Iraq’s removal of PKK-affiliated fighters from Nineveh’s Sinjar, the homeland of the Yazidi minority subjected to the 2014 IS genocide.
Abdullah described Turkey’s willingness to hand over Bashiqa as a “low-cost concession” rather than the start of any strategic withdrawal. Turkey only established its presence there a decade ago to train local forces battling IS. It is also the furthest base from Turkey’s border.
Nevertheless, it’s important since it is linked to a network of forward bases along the border that support Turkey’s broader counter-PKK mission.
“The handover is also a trade, not a gesture,” Abdullah said. “In return, Baghdad committed to establishing full state authority in Sinjar and removing PKK-linked groups."
The agreement also specifies a “gradual handover” tied to security steps taken on the Iraqi side. As a result, the withdrawal timeline is wide open to delay.
“The real test is on the ground,” Abdullah said. “An Iraqi commander expects Bashiqa to be vacated by the end of this year. If it is, that is a genuine signal. A phased withdrawal begins only when the forward bases start closing, not Bashiqa.”
Therefore, statements and agreements don’t reflect reality on the ground. What would be considered a clear signal that the Turkish withdrawal has begun, the ACLED expert added, is an “actual withdrawal on the ground rather than another statement of agreement between the two sides.”
Syria's status quo
Turkey’s support for Syrian government forces in their January offensive against the SDF proved vital. Ankara is still supporting Syrian government forces in their efforts to establish complete authority in hitherto SDF-controlled areas.
The situation remains unsettled, with ACLED’s Abdullah pointing to reports of armed groups, including the PKK-affiliated Revolutionary Youth Movement, opposed to the Damascus-SDF agreement still operating in those areas. Still, Turkey-Syria collaboration isn’t limited to the SDF.
“Basically, while the Turkish concerns are mainly related to the SDF/PKK activities in Syria, it is also related to the IS activities in Syria,” Abdullah said.
“So yes, the nature of the Syrian-Turkish relationship has changed mostly from cross-border operations and military support on the ground to more of intelligence and training collaboration.”
In his interview last week, Guler noted that Turkey has established “close coordination in the field of security” with Syria’s post-Assad authorities and seeks to “strengthen the capacity” of the new armed forces “to ensure the security of our borders.”
“While the al-Sharaa government has been pushing to take full control of the northern border and end Turkish military control there, Ankara has been pushing for at least a measured understanding with Damascus that would allow Turkish military presence to continue,” Ozeren said.
The Orion Policy Institute’s senior fellow contends that if the present Kurdish resolution process ultimately results in the PKK’s total disarmament and the return under amnesty of ex-PKK fighters to Turkey, then Ankara’s pretext for its military presence in Iraq will become unviable.
“However, two developments could alter the security landscape across the region: an expansion of the Saudi-led conflict with Iran-backed Houthis into a regional conflict, and an escalation of the US and Israel war against Iran into ground operations,” Ozeren told The New Arab.
“Such developments would force non-state actors, including PMFs in Iraq and PKK-linked groups in Iran and even Iraq, to reconsider current arrangements.”
That possibility could especially become a reality if Turkey decides to “pursue military involvement” through its commitments under the Mecca Defence Pact.
"If, and this is a big if, Damascus establishes full governance across the country, Turkey’s security- and defence-oriented influence may diminish, as the al-Sharaa government has tried to diversify its defence and military engagements with other actors,” he said.
In September, President al-Sharaa said that his country is “now entering the stage of giving legal status to the Turkish bases in northwestern Syria,” subject to the approval of the Syrian People’s Assembly.
He clarified that Syria does not have a long-term need for such foreign bases but also wants to “maintain diplomatic relations and mutual respect with neighbouring and friendly countries.”
ACLED’s Abdullah assesses that Sharaa’s statement implies that Syria doesn’t want any long-term Turkish presence on its soil to avoid turning the country into an arena of regional conflict.
That is especially urgent considering the growing tension between Turkey and Israel, which could transform Syria into a flashpoint between these two regional heavyweights.
Israel’s repeated targeting of Syrian airbases that Turkey evaluated for potential use demonstrated how quickly Turkey’s presence could potentially draw Syria into a regional confrontation.
“At the same time, Damascus cannot yet do without Turkish support,” Abdullah said. “As-Suweida remains unresolved, and IS and other groups may expand their activity.”
“Legal status for the bases is Damascus’s way of regulating Turkey’s presence now, so it can reduce that presence later."
In early August, Syria reached a memorandum of understanding on the future conditions of Russia’s access to the coastal naval and air bases of Tartus and Hmeimim under which the bases will become joint training centres after a three-month transitional process.
While Abdullah anticipates that’s the direction Damascus is pushing regarding the Turkish presence, he stressed that any comparison with Russia has significant limits.
“Russia’s presence is two bases far from Syria’s borders, and their value to Moscow is regional reach," he said. “Turkey’s presence sits on a 900-km land border and is tied to a security concern Ankara considers existential. That makes it much harder to reduce to a residual training mission.”
“Expect a smaller footprint over several years, but not a Turkey that fully leaves northern Syria.”
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.
Follow him on Twitter: @pauliddon

articles.title: GUR discloses data on foreign tech equipment used by Russian ballistic missile makers
articles.body:
The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (GUR) published data on the War&Sanctions portal regarding three dozen units of foreign-made technological equipment used by cooperation enterprises producing Russian ballistic armaments, the GUR press service reported.
"The Russian military-industrial complex retains a significant dependence on foreign technologies. In particular, despite all efforts, Russia is still unable to replace industrial equipment from global manufacturers with localized analogs. Today we are publishing 30 units of technological equipment of Chinese, German, Taiwanese, American, Turkish, Swiss, and Italian manufacture used by Russian factories producing ballistic missiles and their components – altimeters, aerodynamic rudders, gyroscopes, etc. Characteristic is the growing number of Chinese machine tools and machining centers, including five-axis ones," the message on Telegram reads.
It is noted that Chinese machine tools utilize European, Japanese, and Taiwanese components – CNC systems, servo drives, high-precision spindles and bearings, measuring and rotary systems, linear guides, thermal stabilization tools, and machining process control systems, among others.
The publication notably includes a 5-axis universal machining center GX-650 manufactured by Hyper Machine Tool (PRC), used by Votkinsk Plant – a manufacturer of 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile; Shtral (PRC) turning and milling machining centers involved in the production processes of JSC PEMZ Molot, which produces electronic equipment units for Iskander-M missiles; and measuring equipment from German manufacturer Rohde & Schwarz installed at UPKB Detal, which produces altimeters for Zircon missiles.
GUR reminded that in order to deprive the aggressor of the capability to continue the war, it is necessary, in particular: to strengthen end-user control and the actual location of product use, including introducing on-site inspections by authorized representatives at the declared equipment installation address; and to extend enhanced control procedures to spare parts, components, technical fluids, consumables, software, updates, and maintenance required for equipment operation.
GUR also noted that it is necessary to regularly conduct audits of distributors, dealers, and other intermediaries, especially those supplying to high-risk jurisdictions, as well as to identify signs of re-export or end-user changes, investigate cases where a manufacturer's products are detected in the Russian military-industrial complex, establish their supply chains, and take measures to halt further deliveries through relevant intermediaries.
In addition, it is necessary to restrict deliveries of CNCs, tools, and other components to Chinese manufacturers that supply their equipment to Russian military-industrial complex enterprises, the message states.

articles.title: Ukraine Extends Martial Law and Mobilization Until Jan. 29
articles.body:
Ukraine has extended martial law and general mobilization for another 90 days, until Jan. 29, 2027, as Russia’s full-scale invasion continues in its fifth year.
Since February 2022, both measures have been renewed every three months. On Monday, Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky signed laws No. 5029-IX on martial law and No. 5030-IX on mobilization after they were approved by the parliament on the same day.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Both laws take effect on Oct. 31, when the current extension expires, Ukrinform reported.
Decrees cite ongoing Russian aggression
The laws Zelensky signed approve two presidential decrees; No. 1060/2026 on extending martial law and No. 1061/2026 on extending general mobilization, which required parliament’s consent to take effect.
The martial law decree points to Russia’s continuing large-scale armed aggression against Ukraine as the reason for the extensions.
It was issued on a proposal from the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC), under Article 106 of Ukraine’s Constitution and the law on the legal regime of martial law. The decree amends Article 1 of Decree No. 64/2022 of Feb. 24, 2022, which first introduced martial law nationwide.
Parliament backs extension
According to Ukrinform, lawmakers approved both measures earlier on Monday, after parliament’s committee on national security, defense and intelligence had endorsed them.
Bill No. 16182, approving the martial law decree, received 293 votes, while Bill No. 16183, covering mobilization, passed with 281 in favor.
Trump’s Diesel Scam Backfires
Speaking in parliament ahead of the vote, NSDC Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine Ihor Klymenko said the extension would help Ukraine take “adequate measures to counter armed aggression.” The move would also safeguard the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, he argued.
According to Klymenko, the extension also keeps in force the special powers held by state authorities, the military command, military administrations and local governments, which they need to repel the invasion.
Deferment rules tightened days earlier
The extension comes days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretsky’s government finalized an overhaul of Ukraine’s worker deferment system on Oct. 23, effectively ending automatic exemptions from mobilization for defense and energy companies.
Unless they qualify for a deferment due to health-related issues or work, Ukrainian law requires men aged 25 to 60 to serve in the military. Under the previous rules, most critical companies could defer up to 50% of their draft-age employees, while defense and energy firms have been allowed to defer up to 100%.
The latest overhaul ends automatic 100% protection and aims to create fair rules for those working away from the front, and, above all, for soldiers who have been fighting for nearly five years and need a realistic chance to return home.
“Unconditional full deferment is unfair to those who serve and opens the door to misuse,” Koretskyi said earlier, adding that some companies had been set up purely to obtain deferments and that “it became a business.”
The new approach makes full protection conditional – companies can keep their entire workforce only in case they contribute to the military on a rotating basis.
“The ultimate goal is that no one has to search for anyone on the streets,” Koretskyi said, in an apparent reference to recruiters forcibly detaining men in public.
Defense manufacturers have already lobbied against the new measures, noting that lowering the quota, even to 85%, could halt production lines, delay weapons deliveries and expose companies to penalties for missing state contract lines.
Speaking at the Kyiv International Economic Forum on Monday, Koretskyi reiterated that Russia could mobilize another 300,000 to 500,000 people. Without planning ahead, he argued, Kyiv could again be forced into unpopular emergency decisions.
On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree No. 700, increasing the size of Russia’s armed forces to 2.4 million, including 1.5 million active-duty military personnel, marking the fourth time such a decree was signed in 2026 alone.
Around the same time, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia had already begun additional mobilization, including the expansion of foreign troops, with over 8,000 already in Russia and up to 50,000 more planned.

articles.title: Germany plans to purchase Ukrainian Bars missiles for Bundeswehr testing – FT
articles.body:
Germany plans to purchase Ukrainian Bars missiles for Bundeswehr testing – FT
The Financial Times reports, citing sources, that Germany is preparing its first purchase of Ukrainian-developed Bars missiles for its military. If the trials are successful, the order could be expanded to several hundred missiles.
Source: Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sources familiar with the plans indicate that the German government is expected to sign an agreement in the coming weeks to purchase an initial batch of Bars missiles for testing by the Bundeswehr.
The Bars is a jet-powered missile with a flight range of up to 1,000 km and a payload capacity of up to 105 kg, depending on the modification.
Although Ukrainians sometimes refer to it as a drone missile, Germany classifies it as a low-cost cruise missile.
The initial batch will enable the German military to conduct technical trials early next year. If the results are satisfactory, this could potentially pave the way for a larger order of several hundred units.
This initiative is part of Germany's comprehensive efforts to bolster European deterrence against Moscow by expanding its arsenal of long-range strike weapons.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described the Bars as one of the weapons used to strike military bases and energy facilities on Russian territory.
In recent months, Bars missiles have also been manufactured in Germany by a joint Ukrainian-German company whose operations remain shrouded in secrecy.
The first batch of German-made Bars missiles, funded by the German side, was delivered to Ukraine in October.
The joint venture will now also produce goods for Germany, marking the first known procurement of Ukrainian-developed offensive weaponry for the Bundeswehr's own needs.
In addition to the Bars missiles, Germany plans to acquire and test a small batch of Anthem cruise missiles produced by the US startup Covenant. The Anthem costs approximately one-tenth the price of a Tomahawk missile, which ranges from US$4 million to US$6 million.
One source familiar with the details stated that the Bars is even cheaper, but the German side is prepared to purchase both systems.
It was also noted that the potential acquisition of the Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile has been postponed for now.
Currently, the German armed forces only use the air-launched Taurus cruise missile, which has a relatively short range of about 500 km. Germany's plan to purchase the powerful BGM-109 Tomahawk missile and the Typhon ground-based launcher system from US manufacturer Raytheon could be delayed for up to five years.
Background:
- Media reports indicate that the German government expects to spend nearly €12 billion to create a new arsenal of long-range weapons designed to deter Russia.
- Recently, Denmark also announced a billion-dollar deal to purchase high-precision long-range missiles for the first time in its history, amid intentions to bolster its security.

articles.title: Germany plans to buy Ukrainian Bars missiles
articles.body:
Germany is preparing to buy Ukrainian-made Bars cruise missiles for its armed forces, the Financial Times reported. An agreement for the first batch is expected to be signed in the coming weeks, and Germany could order several hundred missiles if technical tests succeed.
According to the FT, the missile Germany has chosen is the Bars, which has a range of up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) and a payload of up to 105 kilograms (231 pounds). Ukraine uses the missiles to strike military facilities and energy infrastructure in Russia.
Experts say the Bars is the most widely produced of Ukraine’s low-cost missiles. It accounts for the largest number of launches, and its use has been the most thoroughly refined.
Germany already produces the Bars at a joint Ukrainian-German enterprise created under the Build with Ukraine program. Ukraine received the first batch of missiles made there in October.
Politico reported in late August, citing German Defense Ministry documents, that Berlin plans to spend almost 12 billion euros building an arsenal of long-range weapons to deter Russia.
Under the plan, Germany would spend 1.8 billion euros on low-cost cruise missiles, with three options under consideration: Ukraine’s Bars and Flamingo missiles, and missiles from the American-Israeli startup Covenant Industries.
The agreement would mark the first known instance of the Bundeswehr buying offensive weapons of Ukrainian design for its own use. NATO countries are increasingly considering Ukrainian military technology, the FT said. Denmark, Estonia, and Latvia have also said they are ready to buy Ukrainian weapons.

articles.title: Air defense downs 112 of 140 Russian UAVs, 3 Kh-59/69 missiles; strikes recorded at 15 locations – Air Force
articles.body:
On the night of Monday, October 26, air defense forces shot down and suppressed three Kh-59/69 guided air missiles and 112 out of 140 drones of various types used by Russian troops to attack Ukraine, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Telegram.
"On the night of October 26 (from 18:00 on October 25), Russia attacked with one Kh-31P anti-radiation missile, three Kh-59/69 guided air missiles from the temporarily occupied territories of Zaporizhia and Kherson regions, and 140 Shahed-type strike UAVs (70 of them jet-powered), Gerberas, and 'Parodiya'-type decoy drones from the directions of Orel, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo – Russia, and the TOT of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea – Hvardiyske," the message reads.
According to preliminary data from the military, as of 08:00, air defenses shot down and suppressed three Kh-59/69 guided air missiles and 112 Russian UAVs, including Shahed-type (56 of them jet-powered), "Gerbera," and other drone types.
At the same time, hits by Russian air attack assets were recorded at 15 locations, while the falling of downed targets (debris) was recorded at four locations.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine. As of the morning, the attack is ongoing, with several Russian UAVs remaining in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: Iran says US ‘not serious’ about talks, rejects claims over nuclear program
articles.body:
Iran accused the US on Monday of lacking seriousness in negotiations, saying Washington has repeatedly confused diplomacy with imposing demands on Tehran.
“The American side is not serious about negotiations,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said during his weekly news conference, as cited by the state-run IRNA news agency.
He accused Washington of repeatedly making false claims, recalling that US President Donald Trump had expressed support for negotiations shortly before the US military attacks on Iran in June 2025.
“What do you call this? Do you see any goodwill in this approach?” he asked.
Baqaei said Tehran had not received any new European proposal for negotiations beyond a political statement, criticizing Britain, France and Germany for their positions during the conflict.
He accused the three countries of following Washington’s lead on the restoration of UN sanctions and failing to condemn military attacks against Iran.
 
No nuclear weapons
Baqaei reiterated that Iran had never possessed nuclear weapons or sought to acquire them, accusing Washington of using allegations about Tehran’s nuclear program to justify military action.
He said Iran had negotiated in good faith and signed the 2015 nuclear agreement, but the US withdrew from it three years later.
The spokesman accused the US administration of being influenced by Israeli claims about Iran’s nuclear program, describing allegations that Tehran was developing a nuclear bomb as a justification for military aggression.
 
Missing Iranian pilots
Baqaei said Iran continued to hold Qatar responsible for clarifying the fate of three Iranian pilots whose aircraft were hit in the Gulf country.
“Until we have evidence of their deaths or receive precise information and documentation, we assume that the country where their aircraft were hit must be held accountable,” he said.
He added that Tehran was pursuing the matter in coordination with its military leadership and through technical delegations and legal discussions.
Baqaei also confirmed that a Qatari delegation recently visited Tehran, saying the trip involved bilateral cooperation and regional mediation efforts.
He described such visits as normal during regional conflicts, noting that Qatar had sought to convey messages and present its positions.
Commenting on Israel’s upcoming elections and threats of military action against Iran, Baqaei accused Israeli politicians of competing over who could commit more crimes.
“It makes no difference to us who takes charge of a regime with a history of violence and killings,” he said.
 
Russia visit
The spokesman confirmed that President Masoud Pezeshkian would travel to Russia on Monday night to attend a summit of gas-exporting countries.
He said the visit would provide opportunities to strengthen energy cooperation with Moscow and hold consultations with other major energy-producing countries.
Baqaei also addressed border-related difficulties with Pakistan and Iraq, saying discussions with Islamabad were progressing positively.
He said Pakistan had described the issue as technical while also raising security concerns, including reports of planned attacks.
Regarding Iraq, he said Iranian diplomatic missions were pursuing the matter, warning that US pressure on Baghdad could harm the Iraqi population and bilateral relations.
Baqaei said Iran summoned the Italian ambassador on Sunday to express concern over the authorities’ handling of protests in European countries.
He accused France, Belgium and Italy of using excessive force and restricting the right to protest, saying such measures were inconsistent with their human rights obligations.
The French ambassador had also been summoned previously, he added.
 
Saudi Arabia and Yemen
On the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Baqaei said regional security was interconnected and instability in one country could affect others.
He stressed that the dispute should be resolved between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, reiterating Tehran’s readiness to help facilitate a settlement.
“Military approaches make problems more complicated and cause extensive damage,” he said, expressing hope that Saudi Arabia would pursue a negotiated solution.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have persisted since the US and Israel launched military attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a regional conflict and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
On June 18, Trump and Pezeshkian signed a Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding, aimed at ending hostilities, reopening the strategic waterway and paving the way for a broader agreement.
However, disagreements over the implementation of the understanding, including the US naval blockade, sanctions and navigation through the strait, have continued to hinder diplomatic efforts.
Earlier this month, Iran said restoring security to the Strait of Hormuz remained central to negotiations with Washington, insisting that the US must take specific steps to resolve the standoff.

articles.title: General Staff confirmed the striking of Russian facilities producing missile components
articles.body:
General Staff confirmed the striking of Russian facilities producing missile components
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Energia plant and facilities in Oryol, Donetsk, and Tolyatti. The strikes complicate the production of missiles and drones.
On October 26, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed the strike on the Energia plant in Yelets and the results of the strikes on Proton-Elektroteks and Tolyattikauchuk, UNN writes.
Details
According to the General Staff, "on October 25 and during the night of October 26, units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck":
-  "the workshop producing power sources for the enemy’s weapons at the Energia enterprise in the city of Yelets, Lipetsk region, rf. A fire broke out on the enterprise’s premises". 
The strike, as stated, complicates the rf army’s production of power sources for missiles, guided aerial bombs, and other weapons. "Energia" is the only manufacturer of batteries for guidance and correction modules for aerial bombs, and also produces batteries for Iskander-M operational-tactical missile systems and sea-launched cruise missiles.
Following the previous strikes, the General Staff reported that the following had been confirmed:
-  "the main microchip production workshop was destroyed, and the building and servers of the Proton-Elektroteks enterprise in the city of Orel, Orel region, rf, were damaged. The strike took place on October 23". 
This, as noted, complicates the enemy’s production of components for cruise and ballistic missiles with which it strikes Ukrainian cities.
-  "a storage, preparation, and launch site for attack UAVs in the Donetsk area, struck on October 23. Three buildings used for preparing and equipping attack UAVs and one launch rail were damaged". 
This, as noted, reduces the enemy’s capabilities to attack Ukraine and civilian infrastructure with drones of various modifications.
-  "the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the city of Tolyatti, Samara region, rf, struck on October 24. A process pipeline, two butyl rubber production units, and one rectification unit were damaged". 
This, as reported, strikes at the production chain for solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.
"The Defense Forces of Ukraine are striking the enemy’s military facilities within the framework of the right to self-defense guaranteed by Article 51 of the UN Charter," the General Staff emphasized.

articles.title: Pezeshkian to Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi officials: Iran seeks cooperation, will defend rights
articles.body:
Pezeshkian to Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi officials: Iran seeks cooperation, will defend rights
TEHRAN – Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — the three countries that recently signed the Mecca defense pact — traveled to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met with President Masoud Pezeshkian and with Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
Speaking at a joint meeting with the three visiting officials, President Pezeshkian welcomed dialogue among Islamic countries and stressed the failure of enemies to achieve their objectives against Iran.
"They imagined they could bring the Islamic Republic of Iran to collapse through pressure and aggression; but the result of these actions was the strengthening of internal unity and cohesion and increased solidarity of the Iranian nation," Pezeshkian said.
"Our people, despite the imposed losses and hardships, defended their land with power and steadfastness. The notion that the Iranian nation can be forced into surrender is a false and void notion," he added.
The president said the Islamic Republic of Iran pursues its legal rights within the principles and rules of international law, and relying on those very principles, will firmly defend the legitimate rights and interests of the Iranian nation.
Call for united front against Israel
Pezeshkian expressed hope that the presence of major and influential Islamic countries could play an effective role in strengthening regional stability and unity.
"We should not allow the Zionist regime to commit terror and aggression against any individual or country whenever it wishes. I am confident that if Islamic countries stand together and adopt a coordinated position, such actions cannot be repeated," he said.
"I believe that if we manage our differences and emphasize commonalities and shared interests instead of focusing on divisive issues, we can overcome regional problems more easily and effectively," he added.
He warned against interventionist and divisive policies, saying one of the objectives pursued in the policies of the US and the Zionist regime is to weaken regional countries, create rifts among Muslim nations and gradually weaken major Islamic states.
"We must, by strengthening mutual cooperation and supporting one another, prevent the realization of such objectives and not allow regional countries to be exposed separately to pressure and threats," Pezeshkian said.
He added that Islamic countries should move to meet each other's needs through constructive engagement, economic cooperation and the use of mutual capacities. "The notion that nations can be forced into surrender through pressure and sanctions is a void notion. The deeper and broader cooperation among regional countries becomes, the greater their ability to manage problems and confront external pressures will be."
Pezeshkian stressed that Iran, relying on domestic efforts, the support of the nation and the guidance of the Leader, will successfully pass through difficulties, adding that Islamic countries must understand the interconnectedness of their security and interests. Weakening any major regional country, he said, could pave the way for increased pressure and threats against other Islamic countries as well.
From words to joint action
Emphasizing the need for consistency between words and deeds in regional relations, Pezeshkian said: "We should not say what we do not believe in or fail to uphold in practice. We must, hand in hand, provide the ground for flourishing the region's scientific, economic, cultural, political and security capacities; develop communication routes, facilitate travel, turn borders into opportunities for cooperation and link the universities, scientific centers, traders and merchants of Islamic countries to one another."
He said expanding multilateral cooperation lays the ground for sustainable security, noting: "When science, culture, trade and economy cross borders and communications among nations expand, the ground for the spread of terrorism and insecurity will disappear. Therefore, strengthening scientific, cultural and economic bonds not only helps the development and welfare of nations, but is one of the most effective ways to consolidate collective security in the region."
Pezeshkian said any understanding reached in such meetings that leads to stronger regional unity, cohesion and cooperation will enjoy Iran's serious and all-out support, adding that focus must be placed on common ground and areas of cooperation and differences must not be allowed to hinder shared interests.
Nuclear rights and double standards
In another part of his remarks, Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran's principled position on nuclear activities, saying the Islamic Republic is not seeking nuclear weapons and, as a member of the NPT, wants to continue its nuclear activities within the framework of international rights and obligations.
"Iran accordingly reserves the right to benefit from peaceful nuclear activities and expects these rights to be respected within the framework of international regulations," he said.
He criticized dual approaches toward Iran, saying: "Using the nuclear issue as a pretext for exerting pressure, threats, attacks on nuclear facilities, and claiming readiness for talks and dialogue simultaneously with attacking Iran is a contradictory and unconstructive approach that has undermined public trust and increased distrust among Iranian officials and people."
Pezeshkian said Islamic countries must, by strengthening their interactions and coordination, not allow such approaches to become a routine for dealing with regional nations. Safeguarding nations' rights, respecting countries' sovereignty, countering aggression and strengthening regional cooperation require common will and coordinated action, he added.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran is also ready, relying on religious commonalities, mutual interests and respect for nations' rights, to expand its cooperation with Islamic countries in this path," he said.
The officials of the three neighboring countries also held separate meetings with SNSC Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. At the end of the meetings, the four countries issued a joint press statement, stressing: "The participants agreed to continue talks to strengthen cooperation among the four regional countries, including in the field of peace and security in the region."

articles.title: Drones keep sinking ships off Romania and Bulgaria—French and US patrol planes are watching
articles.body:
French and US maritime patrol planes are watching the western Black Sea, where drones keep hitting merchant ships, Romanian outlet Curs de Guvernare reported on 19 October, citing flight-tracking data. Romania blames Russia for the attacks, while Bulgaria says it cannot prove who launched them.
Ukraine’s three small Danube ports have kept its grain exports from collapsing further, and Russia has pounded those ports since the summer. The ships serving them are now being hit in the economic zones of two NATO members. Many were anchored near or heading to the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube to the sea. That puts the allied patrols over these waters in the middle of the fight over Ukraine’s grain trade.
Two patrol planes over the western Black Sea
A French Navy Atlantique 2 maritime patrol plane arrived in Constanța, Romania’s main Black Sea port, on the evening of 18 October, Curs de Guvernare said. On 24 October, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said in the Bulgarian port of Varna that a French patrol plane had been operating in the area under NATO for two weeks and had contributed to rescue operations.
Two tankers burn off Romania’s Sulina as Bulgaria says it lacks proof Russia is behind the Black Sea ship attacks
Meanwhile, a US Navy P-8A Poseidon flew into Varna from Sicily on 18 October, AFP reported, citing flight-tracking data. Two days later, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said it had begun reconnaissance patrols after Sofia asked allies for help, and that some allies had responded quickly. Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov called the deployment a joint decision of Bulgaria and NATO. He said the plane cannot strike targets and passes its data to NATO, Anadolu Agency reported.
NATO promises more
On 20 October, NATO’s North Atlantic Council met at Romania’s request. Afterward, the alliance said it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones to the Black Sea. NATO military spokesman Col. Martin O’Donnell added that allies have sent or will send intelligence personnel and explosives-forensics teams. NATO itself has not attributed the attacks to any country.
Romania names Russia, Bulgaria hedges
Romania has been blunter. On 15 October, after four merchant ships were hit within a day, acting Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu wrote on X that “Russia bears full responsibility for these developments.” On 17 October, Romanian F-16s shot down two jet-powered Russian Geran drones near Sulina, Romania’s Defense Ministry said.
On 23 October, a drone sank the cargo ship Khoryv off Constanța, killing a Ukrainian sailor, and President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia too. “It is part of Russia’s escalation process in its war in Ukraine,” Dan said.
Bulgaria is more cautious. Radev told parliament on 14 October that the attacks worked in Russia’s favor but that Sofia could not prove it. Since taking office in May, he has sought a thaw in ties with Moscow.

- Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses

articles.title: Copy-paste from Brussels: The EU’s error-riddled new sanctions package was generated using an LLM
articles.body:
The European Union’s latest sanctions package, adopted Oct. 12, bears signs of having been generated by a large language model. The document contains numerous errors — including references to companies that have long since closed, individuals listed without birthdates, and pseudonyms used in place of real names. The package also omits Chinese companies entirely, despite China’s growing role in helping Russia evade sanctions aimed at hindering the work of Moscow’s military-industrial complex amid the war in Ukraine.
The EU’s latest sanctions package is riddled with errors that are striking to the human eye: the mixing of Latin and Cyrillic characters (as in the phrase «Акcionерное общество», or “Joint-stock company”), names listed without birthdates, actors’ stage names used in place of real surnames, and references to companies that ceased operating long ago. While technical mistakes are inevitable in a document covering 1,500 individuals and legal entities, the latest package stands out for the apparent lack of care in its preparation. One of the clearest signs is what appears to be the use of large language models (LLMs) in drafting parts of the text.
“Workslop” and copy-pasting instead of meticulous bureaucracy
At first glance, the use of boilerplate language may not seem significant. Council Decision No. 2026/2279 relies on just two standard phrases to justify sanctions against 1,569 individuals and organizations. That marks a clear departure from previous sanctions packages, which generally included a specific explanation for why each newly designated person or entity had been targeted.
Additionally, for the first time, the EU writes the names of all legal entities as literal transliterations from Russian rather than as they appear in Russia’s official register of legal entities. When Russian organizations are registered, the database typically includes both their full and abbreviated Russian names as well as the English-language name chosen by the organization itself. Some companies use a transliteration in that field, while others provide an actual translation.
In the latest sanctions document, however, company names appear to have been transliterated mechanically and with little quality control. Capitalization was omitted throughout. While similar formatting errors had appeared occasionally in earlier EU sanctions lists, in the latest package nearly every legal entity contains the same type of error.
The transliteration itself is also inconsistent. Different systems appear to have been used for different entries. In most cases, the latest package appears to rely not on a standard transliteration system for Cyrillic but on output generated by the Python library transliterate, with apostrophes subsequently removed. Names of individuals, meanwhile, were generally rendered using the British-American BGN/PCGN system, though not consistently and sometimes with further modifications.
The document is also inconsistent in deciding when to translate Russian names, when to transliterate them, and when to do both at once. One example is the address of Neva-Ferrit LLC. The original address — “198320, St. Petersburg, Krasnoe Selo, Svobody St., 50” — was rendered as “98320, city Sankt-Peterburg, city Krasnoe village, ul. Svobody, bld.50.”
The result mixes translation and transliteration in a way that makes little sense. The place name “Krasnoe Selo,” which should normally remain a proper name, was partially translated into English as “Krasnoe village,” while the street name “Svobody” was left transliterated rather than rendered as “Freedom Street” or “Street of Freedom.”
One possible explanation is that large language models were used to generate parts of the document. That could also account for the apparent use of a Python transliteration library — when asked to automate a task of this kind, an AI system may generate a script, and such a script would likely rely on an existing software library.
If a Python library was in fact used to transliterate company names, that would explain some of the unusual spellings. It would not, however, explain instances in which Latin and Cyrillic characters appear within the same word, such as in the name of the Kalinovsky Chemical Plant: «Акcionерное общество калиновский химический завод».
Similar errors have appeared in earlier sanctions documents, but those usually involved letters that look identical in the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets — such as A, B, T and E. In those cases, the mistake was invisible to the eye but detectable by software and most likely resulted from a person typing without switching the keyboard layout.
The latest document is different. The mixing of alphabets within a single word is more consistent with errors that occur in text generated by neural networks, especially when a task requires several languages to be handled at once.
Another example is the English-language address given for CJSC Tehkrim: “Address: 426063, Udmurtskaya Republic of …” A human translator or conventional machine-translation system would be unlikely to produce that wording, as the standard English form is “Udmurt Republic.”
While a human translator would be unlikely to translate the phrase with such an awkward rendering, a large language model, which does not translate strictly word for word but predicts the most likely sequence of words, certainly could. Because many Russian regions are rendered in English using the construction “Republic of …,” a model could plausibly predict that “of” should follow the name of a Russian republic even where that order is incorrect.
The careless transliteration appears to have affected website addresses as well. For example, the website listed for LLC NPO AMB — rendered by EU sanctions officials as “Obschestvo s ogranichennoj otvetstvennostju Nauchno-proizvodstvennoe obedinenie amb” — became https://www.licenzia-gos.rf. The problem is obvious: the top-level domain “.rf” does not exist. Nor does the listed website exist in that form, or even in the corresponding Cyrillic version, лицензия-гос.рф.
Factories of days gone by
A telling example of an anachronism on the list involves the imposition of sanctions on the Federal State Unitary Enterprise “Novosibirsk Experimental Plant of Measuring Instruments” (TIN / INN 5425100089) and its director, Aleksey Timofeevich Morozov (designation no. 2549, TIN / INN 542505153869). However, this legal entity no longer exists, as it was reorganised in 2021 through a merger with the Federal State Unitary Enterprise “National Testing Association ‘State Ammunition Testing Ranges of Russia’” (TIN / INN 5023002050). That organisation was also subject to sanctions, but its CEO, Stanislav Gennadievich Yuzov, was not included on the EU sanctions list.
It is possible to see how such an error arose. Many companies appear to have been added to the list on the following basis:
“The entities concerned appear in a list recently established by the Government of the Russian Federation that identifies them as belonging to the Russian military-industrial complex, and they are therefore entitled to receive subsidies from the Government of the Russian Federation.”
That suggests an AI model or Python script may have been given a source list that, while broadly reflecting the composition of Russia’s military-industrial complex, was not fully up to date. The resulting entries appear not to have been adequately checked by experts.
More importantly, even an up-to-date list would have limited value as a sanctions tool. Companies in Russia’s defense sector generally do not make foreign purchases directly, meaning sanctions against them may have little practical effect on procurement. Instead, separate intermediary firms typically acquire goods on their behalf — a practice The Insider has documented repeatedly, as have other researchers who study Russian military-industrial procurement.
Even a cursory reading of the latest EU package reveals at least 25 discrepancies in the names and legal forms of the organizations on the list, and numerous errors occur when it comes to naming the positions held by individuals coming under restrictions. In some cases, parts of company names are missing, and in most cases, the legal form is incorrectly stated.
For example, Nikolay Nikolaevich Grechushkin (designation no. 2224) was sanctioned as the CEO of Textile Trading Company LLC (TIN / INN 9701054138). However, that position is actually held by Anatoly Mikhailovich Trubin. At the same time, the list correctly lists Trubin’s INN as 592003498702. Grechushkin, for his part, serves as deputy CEO of the company, and his TIN is 253303297804.
Evgeniya Vladimirovna Kovalenko (TIN / INN 525714947515), is listed as the director of JSC “Himreaktiv.” However, the CEO of this company is actually Vladimir Nikolaevich Lyamkin, who holds TIN 525702072428.
OJSC “Radiodetal,” with TIN 1308038496, also appears on the sanctions list. This organization has a different legal entity and a different name — PJSC “Zubovo-Polyansky Radio Component Plant” — which again indicates that the data used is outdated.
The list also includes the “Federal State Institution Federal Scientific Center Research Institute for Systems Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences” (original spelling retained) with TIN 7727086772. This is also an anachronism. This institute was transferred from the jurisdiction of the Russian Academy of Sciences to the Kurchatov Institute Research Center on Feb. 7, 2023, by Decree No. 268-r of the Government of the Russian Federation. Its current name is “Federal State Autonomous Institution ‘Federal Scientific Center Research Institute for Systems Studies of the National Research Center “Kurchatov Institute”’.”
Sanctioning everyone with the same name — and missing the mark
As previously noted by investigative journalist Sergei Ezhov, EU officials failed to specify the patronymic, date of birth, or taxpayer identification number of Promsvyazbank CEO Mikhail Dorofeev when imposing sanctions against him, thereby creating risks for all people named “Mikhail Dorofeev” worldwide. When compiling the new list, the European Commission expanded this practice: in fact, in the case of the 743 individuals on the current sanctions list, none are supplemented with a date of birth or passport number. However, tax identification numbers (INNs) are listed — something that was previously rare on lists of sanctioned individuals.
The absence of birth dates and passport numbers significantly increases the risk of false matches or missed matches during automated sanctions screening. When processing a Schengen or other visa application, consular officials typically verify an applicant’s passport information and date of birth, but not a Russian taxpayer identification number. After all, if a person is not publicly linked to a Russian company as a founder or director, authorities may have no reliable way to match a TIN to that individual using open-source records, as such information is not generally public. (The same problem can arise in bank compliance checks, which typically rely on a person’s full name and transliterations, date of birth, passport details, address, job title and employer — but not a Russian TIN.)
The Insider has already seen the consequences of this approach: one of our employees was temporarily unable to receive their salary simply due to the fact that they share a surname with a person added to the latest sanctions list, prompting the bank to freeze the payment.
Previously, journalists had repeatedly pointed out factual errors made by European officials when compiling sanctions lists. For example, the EU imposed sanctions on comedian Mikhail Galustyan by using his stage name (the artist’s official name is Nshan). An error was also made regarding his date of birth: Galustyan was born in 1979, not in 1970, as stated in the EU Council’s implementing regulation. These errors have not been corrected a year and a half after the document’s publication.
These oversights may seem minor, but they can have serious legal consequences for EU authorities. In May 2025, for example, an EU court lifted sanctions against Andrei Kharkovsky, described as a “representative of the Cossack Union,” after Brussels failed to establish his connection to the organization. The sanctions listing did not include his date of birth or other identifying information sufficient to distinguish him unambiguously.
Documents such as the October package are examples of “Potemkin sanctions.” They create the appearance of intense activity, and the sheer scale of the lists might impress an outside observer. In reality, however, the latest package completely ignores the Chinese manufacturers and banks that continue to supply Putin’s war machine.
The elephant in the room: Brussels ignores China
Investigations by The Insider and other publications have repeatedly pointed to China’s leading role in the supply of critical goods to Russia. It is Chinese manufacturers and their affiliated Chinese banks — not intermediary exporters or importers — that represent the potential bottlenecks in Russian factories’ supply chains.
The Insider has identified several bottlenecks in a series of investigations related to long-range unmanned systems, such as the Geran attack drone and the Gerbera decoy drone, as well as the mass production of first-person-view (FPV) drones. Both are absolutely critical to the Russian war machine. About 70% of combat losses result from the use of FPV drones, while civilians and civilian infrastructure suffer the most from Geran drones.
Not a single Chinese company — neither manufacturers nor resellers — was included among the hundreds of companies listed in the latest round of EU sanctions. Given the documented role that Chinese products play in the Russian military-industrial complex, the absence of Chinese entities suggests that Brussels lacks the political will to address the driving force sustaining the Russian war machine: imports from Chinese suppliers.

Kyiv • UNN

articles.title: ‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered future
articles.body:
A future Royal Air Force will rely on “autonomy not flesh”, its chief said on Monday as he described plans in which Typhoon fighters are accompanied by four AI-enabled drones capable of patrolling hundreds of miles in the distance.
The technological shift would revolutionise warfare, limit the role of military personnel “towards the outside” and ease the pressure on recruitment, Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth said in a speech in London.
The senior military officer was setting out a strategy for the RAF, which has been told it must be ready to fight against Russia by 2030, at a time when the use of artificial intelligence by the US, Israel, Russia and Ukraine has made warfare more deadly.
“AI will enable warfare that speeds well beyond human comprehension, meaning that our role will shift towards the outside, and it will shift towards controlling the activity and setting the guardrails,” Smyth said.
The aim, he added, was to mirror the Anglo-American second world war model of “steel, not flesh” – relying on tanks and combat aircraft rather than infantry – to avoid the bloody trench warfare that had led to millions of deaths in the first world war.
“Given today’s changing character of war, I would argue strongly that the modern paradigm must now become autonomy, not flesh,” the chief of air staff said in a lecture at the Royal United Services Institute.
Few examples were given about the future use of AI by the air force, but Smyth did point to the £300m Storm Fighter programme of “loyal wingman” drones announced in July as part of the delayed defence investment plan. “Crewed platforms are no longer enough,” Smyth said.
Four armed, AI-enabled uncrewed craft would work alongside every RAF Typhoon, with the first tests to be conducted next year. The aim is for the drones to be in service by the end of the decade, in line with a Nato directive for the UK and other alliance members to be ready to fight Russia if necessary by 2030.
Over the weekend Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the UK had “a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win”.
The drones would “provide force multiplier function and the affordable mass we so definitely require” and, Smyth added, would be “placing sensors, weapons, and united warfare capabilities well within contested airspace”.
One possibility would be to use the drones to track Russian aircraft seeking to cross the Greenland-Ireland-UK gap into the north Atlantic, controlling them from a cockpit of a Typhoon flying over Scotland, several hundred miles away.
AI has been used by the Israeli and US military to dramatically increase the pace of target selection in the wars in Gaza and Iran, allowing them to run more bombing missions.
The IDF used two databases, Lavender and Habsora (or the Gospel), to increase the pace at which it could attack people and buildings during the war in Gaza. The US’s Maven Smart System, developed in conjunction with Palantir, was used to identify and strike 1,000 targets in Iran in the first 24 hours of the war this spring.
Russia and Ukraine have begun to use AI to identify and strike targets on the ground, eliminating the need for satellite or radio communication as they descend on their bombing mission. In July, Ukrainian investigators concluded that a drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was relying on AI for its attack.
“Autonomous air systems penetrate Russia’s perceived sense of sanctuary on a routine basis,” Smyth said, describing how Ukrainian drones conduct long-range strikes against targets inside Russia, such as oil refineries.
Drones would allow the RAF to increase its ability to strike at a time when recruitment has been challenging. The RAF’s fully trained personnel numbers have fallen from 29,800 in 2020 to 27,850 today, and the total has only begun to increase over the last 18 months.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian plant producing missile and bomb batteries in Yelets, General Staff says
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Russian plant producing missile, bomb batteries in Yelets, General Staff says
A fire broke out on the territory of the Energia plant following an overnight attack on the battery plant in the city of Yelets in western Russia overnight on Oct. 26, Ukraine's General Staff said later that day.
The plant is the sole Russian manufacturer of batteries for glide bomb guidance and correction modules, the General Staff said without specifying the extent of the damage.
It added that the plant, located about 250 kilometers (about 155 miles) from Ukraine, also produces batteries for Iskander-M ballistic missile systems and sea-based cruise missiles.
"The strike complicates the Russian Federation's military's production of power sources for missiles, guided bombs, and other weapons," the General Staff said in its Telegram post.
Earlier on Oct. 25, Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova Plus reported that smoke rose over the whole territory of the Energia plant after several missiles appeared to have hit it in the afternoon. The General Staff has not specified what weapons were used to strike the Energia plant in Russia.
In its statement, the General Staff said that Ukraine had also "destroyed" the main microchip production workshop of Proton-Electrotex Enterprise in Orel, western Russia, on Oct. 23. It added that the attack would likely complicate the Russian production of components used to produce cruise and ballistic missiles, which are often deployed to target Ukrainian cities.
The Russian Defense Ministry has not reacted to the General Staff's statement. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claim.
The attack comes as Ukraine intensifies its long-range attacks inside Russia and across Russian-occupied territories, often targeting defense industrial plants, airfields, and oil refineries.
Earlier on Oct. 26, independent Russian media outlet Astra reported that a chemical plant producing dual-use goods in the southwestern Russian city of Voronezh was likely hit in a Ukrainian drone attack.

articles.title: Israel’s Mossad chief backed swift Iran operation opposed by army chief: Report
articles.body:
The head of Israeli spy agency the Mossad backed a swift military operation against Iran proposed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir opposed it, Israeli media reported Monday, on the eve of the country’s pivotal general elections, with Netanyahu’s post at stake, Anadolu reports.
Daily Israel Hayom said Netanyahu pushed for the operation but faced opposition from Zamir, who had not been informed of it in advance, while Mossad chief Roman Gofman supported the proposal.
The daily quoted an unnamed source familiar with the discussions as saying the operation “could have led to renewed war with Iran,” although it would not have amounted to a resumption of an intensive military offensive.
Israeli opposition figures accused Netanyahu over the past week of seeking to attack Iran to influence the election results. However, an Israeli military official told the newspaper that the proposed operation did not involve restarting a large-scale offensive.
An attack of that scale would only take place with full coordination between Israel and the US and a decision by US President Donald Trump, rather than by Israel alone, the official said.
According to the newspaper, Israeli and foreign officials believe a large-scale attack on Iran is inevitable, citing what they called Tehran’s progress toward acquiring a nuclear bomb, with the remaining question being its timing.
The timing would depend primarily on operational and intelligence considerations aimed at preventing Iran from reaching a point of no return in developing a nuclear weapon, the report said.
Diplomatic sources told the daily that Trump wants to wait until after the US’ Nov. 3 midterm elections, believing an attack could be carried out just as effectively later.
They also cited concerns that an attack could drive oil prices higher and hurt the election results.
The newspaper also reported that Israel and the US are preparing a plan to bring down the Iranian government.
READ: Former Iranian President Ahmadinejad denies report alleging Mossad contacts
Reported row
On Sunday evening, Israel’s privately owned Channel 12 reported an “unprecedented” confrontation between Netanyahu and Zamir over political directives to carry out a military operation that could quickly lead to a confrontation with Iran.
The channel said the dispute had peaked over the preceding 24 hours, amid concerns within the military establishment that the Iranian issue could be used for political gains ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections.
Netanyahu has placed security issues at the center of his election campaign, while opinion polls suggest his bloc will struggle to secure the parliamentary majority needed to form a government.
On Sunday, he posted an AI-generated image depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv, accompanied by a warning about the danger of Iran acquiring a nuclear weapon and a call to complete the confrontation with Tehran during the two years left in Trump’s term.
Netanyahu has led a far-right government since late 2022, widely described as the most extreme in Israel’s history.
On June 13, 2025, Israel launched a large-scale attack on Iran targeting nuclear and military facilities. Tehran retaliated with missiles and drones before the confrontation ended with a ceasefire that June 24.
Then this Feb. 28, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and what it described as US military facilities in Arab countries.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 and began negotiations that later collapsed over disagreements concerning navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for energy supplies and goods.

articles.title: Iraq suspects Israel behind attack on weapons depots and military systems inside Iraq
articles.body:
An attack targeted military facilities in Iraq last week, including Chinese-made air defence systems and ammunition depots reportedly recently delivered from Iran for Shiite militias in the country, Iraqi sources said, with suspicions that Israel was behind the strike.
Saudi media quoted two Iraqi sources as saying that authorities in Baghdad had indications pointing to Israel’s involvement, but had yet to determine how the attack was carried out or whether it involved warplanes or drones.
The attack wounded five people, who sustained minor injuries, according to the sources. Iraqi authorities are still investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The developments come amid previous reports of possible Israeli military activity inside Iraq. About six months ago, US media reported that Israel had established a secret military base in Iraq, housing special forces and serving as a logistical hub for the Israeli air force, in coordination with the United States, according to sources cited in those reports.

articles.title: For the third time this year, Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s rocket-fuel rubber plant in Samara Oblast. This time they reach the raw-material shop feeding it
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones damaged a process pipeline, two butyl-rubber units, and a rectification (distillation) unit at Russia’s Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant on 24 October, Ukraine’s General Staff said on 26 October. The damage hits the production chain of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles, it added.
The strike was part of a string of Ukrainian hits on Russian plants over four days, most of which the General Staff links to missile production. Ukraine hit an electronics plant in Oryol on 23 October and struck a battery plant in Yelets on 25 October or the following night. The General Staff ties both to missiles: Oryol makes components for missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities, and Yelets makes batteries for Iskander-M systems. Then, overnight on 26 October, drones also went after Voronezhsintezkauchuk, another Russian synthetic-rubber plant. For Tolyattikauchuk, this is the third time this year that strikes have reached its butyl-rubber shops.
What Kyiv and Russian officials say
The General Staff first confirmed the strike on 24 October with a report of an explosion and fire near the plant. It said the plant makes synthetic rubbers, monomers, fractions, and high-octane gasoline additives, and that its synthetic rubbers are used in solid rocket fuel.
Meanwhile, Russian officials have not named the plant in their statements. However, Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh claimed that industrial facilities were damaged and, citing preliminary data, that no one was killed or injured, Russian outlet Expert reported.
What OSINT channels report
Drones hit at least two production facilities, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said. One is the shop where isobutane is turned into isobutylene, a raw material for synthetic rubbers. The other is outdoor unit No. 2 in shop BK-4, which produces and purifies high-purity isobutylene for butyl rubber.
The damage could delay rubber output and the supply of feedstock for other processes, including solid rocket fuel. Tolyattikauchuk can make about 260,000 metric tons of synthetic rubber a year, OSINT-Varta data show.
Hit again and again
Tolyattikauchuk had come under fire before. Overnight on 4 April, about 10 drones reached the plant by various accounts. Footage showed fires at storage shops D-12 and D-1 and at the BK-2, BK-3, and BK-4 units, though more sites may have been hit, the analysts added. Ukrainian forces struck the plant again on 12 June, the General Staff confirmed.
Then, on 12 September, a strike set fires at the BK-2, BK-3, and BK-4 shops, an OSINT community Absolutely Reliable Source reported. Without those shops running steadily, the line that makes MTBE, a key high-octane gasoline additive, is cut, the channel noted.
