articles.title: I saw a drone suddenly descend towards me. My heart started pounding and I thought, ‘Is this the end of my life?’
articles.body:
It was mid-April and after a month of deadly airstrikes across Lebanon, Israel agreed to a ceasefire. Much of the bombing had focused on southern Lebanon, where entire villages had been demolished. But with the truce, people were hopeful of being able to return to their homes or to see what remained.
Zeinab Faraj, a 21-year-old photojournalist, decided to join Amal Khalil, 42, a newspaper reporter in Lebanon, on a trip to an area in the south of the country to document the aftermath of war. The two had worked together on a number of assignments after Khalil had seen Faraj’s work on social media and contacted her.
“I expected it to be like every other time. Amal and I would go out, take some footage and then leave. I had absolutely no sense of fear. We could hear some gunfire and artillery, but as a videographer, you find those things important to document and capture,” says Faraj, who was freelancing alongside finishing her degree in radio and TV.
By the time they reached the village of al-Tiri on the afternoon of 22 April, Faraj began to look out the window and reminisce. She was born and grew up in the nearby city of Bint Jbeil. “My whole life revolved around this area. As we say, a fish suffocates when it’s taken out of water. That’s how we feel whenever we leave Bint Jbeil.”
Ahead of them was a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, 27, a municipal official in Bint Jbeil, and Mohammed Hourani, 37, a friend of the mayor. They had met them by chance earlier in the day at Tebnine governmental hospital, which had become a gathering point because people considered it relatively safe and would base their movements from there. Bazzi was due to sign a marriage contract that evening, but was still keen to join the trip.
Faraj says she did not hear the missile coming, just the sound of Khalil screaming and then the sight of the car in front of them on fire. The two women got out of their car.
“I do not know how I managed to stay so calm. The only thing I could think was: if I come closer, I will be able to see Ali. Maybe I will be able to pull him out.”
Khalil kept repeating: “Oh God, they’re gone.” Slowly, Faraj began to understand what was going on. “I could see their bodies torn apart.”
Then the drones appeared.
“When the drones came, my heart started pounding in a terrifying way. The drone started coming very close to my face. I tried to cover my face, but whenever I did, it would fly back up. That was when I really felt the real danger.”
The drones flew low and close as Khalil and Faraj frantically made phone calls to emergency services who repeatedly assured them that help was on its way. Faraj says the assurances were “like an anaesthetic”, something that briefly numbed the reality that no one was rescuing them.
One of the paramedics on a call told them to get into their car and try to drive back up the road, as ambulances were being preventing from driving to where they were. But as they tried to get into the car, it was struck by a missile.
Both of them were thrown backwards, with Khalil wrapping her arms around Faraj. As the drone continued to circle overhead, Khalil said she hoped it would “think we were dead”.
With the nearby car engulfed in flames, they decided to take shelter in a nearby house. Khalil had visible injuries, with blood on her face, hand and leg. Faraj says she sent her sister a last message before her phone died: “There’s no hope left. Forgive me.”
Inside, they sat on a bathroom floor. Khalil was unable to move, so Faraj says she crawled to a position from where she could watch the road. Suddenly a drone descended towards her.
“It had been high up and suddenly it came down. The way it descended was terrifying. My heart stopped.” Soon after this, Faraj says she came back inside and began to feel tired and detached from what was happening. “I felt alone.”
Then came the sound of a missile falling. “I’ve never heard anything like it in my life. I’ve heard so many strikes and drones, but this was completely different. It was terrifying and Amal was screaming,” she says.
She does not remember what happened next, but when she opened her eyes an enormous weight was pressing down on her body. Everything was black and she could barely breathe. She was trapped underneath rubble. “I couldn’t bear the weight. It felt like something was pushing me down, crushing me. All I cared about was being able to breathe.”
Faraj says she then heard a voice and thought it was her father, but it was a paramedic who had managed to reach the scene of the attack. As he held her by the shoulders, Faraj says she instinctively clung to him and refused to let go. “I told him: ‘Don’t leave me. I’m afraid to stay alone.’” He stayed beside her while a second paramedic cleared the rubble.
As the sound of drones returned once more, the paramedics quickly pulled Faraj free as she screamed from the pain. At about the same time, Faraj says she heard a stun grenade dropped by the drone. As they drove away in the ambulance, she repeatedly mistook the sound of the vehicle for a drone. “They’re going to hit us. We’re not going to make it,” she says she kept repeating.
After they got to a hospital, Faraj says she started to ask about Khalil. At first the nurses tried to reassure her. But eventually, she says, they fell silent. “That’s when I knew she was gone.” Khalil is believed to have died about an hour before the paramedics had been allowed to return to the area again after rescuing Faraj.
The Israeli military justified their attack saying they had identified saboteurs violating the ceasefire. However, human rights groups called it a war crime. As Khalil and Faraj took refuge in the building the Israeli military received repeated messages urging them to allow a rescue operation. A week before the attack, an Israeli military spokesperson shared a video of Khalil published by her newspaper and described it as “terrorist media”. Khalil had also received death threats from Israeli numbers.
Today, as Faraj prepares to return to university, she still struggles to walk properly and has visible injuries to a hand. An injury to her face has affected the movement of one eyebrow; others are hidden by her clothes and hijab. Her limp is especially hard to bear. “I was always on the move. I lost that. Even climbing stairs can be hard,” she says.
At first she was in shock, she says, but now more symptoms are starting to appear. She wakes at night screaming and buries herself in the pillows as if a missile is going to strike. The sound of drones and warplanes put her on edge.
Returning to frontline journalism feels uncertain and she says she is repeatedly haunted by the image of Hourani lying on the ground after the first missile attack. “His head was turned towards me. His eyes open and looking at me. That is something I will never get out of my head.”

articles.title: Fewer than half of Ukraine’s F-16s may be operational. Kyiv wants newer Block 70/72 jets to face Russia’s Su-35 fighters, Air Force says
articles.body:
Ukraine is remaking its air force on NATO’s model, down to the way its squadrons are organized and the aircraft they fly. The reforms are planned to be completed by 2035 and include modernizing its F-16s while pursuing the Swedish Gripen jets, Air Force Spokesperson Yurii Ihnat says, per Tse Baza.
Ukraine’s fighters are working hard against Russia’s air war, and in the previous month alone the Air Force faced around 3,500 jet-powered targets, with F-16s heavily used to intercept Russian drones. The new reform is meant to build an air force that can be sustained over the long term and can contest Russian jets and glide bombs, not only survive the next wave.
Wings and universal air bases
The central change, Ihnat said, is a move to the “wing” units that NATO air forces use. The first steps have already been taken: Ukraine has set up the 107th F-16 wing, which now has its own Facebook page and may publish material about its work.
Ukraine also plans to build universal air bases on the operational airfields it has used through the full-scale war. In the future, Ihnat says, those bases should be able to receive and service different models of combat aircraft, as NATO does.
A worn fleet, and the jets Ukraine wants next
Currently, the F-16s Ukraine flies are older Block 15 jets, used by other countries before they arrived, and intensive combat has left them in need of repairs, service life restoration, and upgrades.
Ukrainian officials discussed modernization with the American manufacturer Lockheed Martin, while Kyiv would prefer the newer Block 70/72 version, which Ihnat says would let its pilots stand up more confidently to Russia’s Su-35 fighters.
Keeping the current fleet flying has been hard: fewer than half of Ukraine’s F-16s may be operational, held back by slow maintenance abroad.
At the same time, Lockheed Martin and Kyiv are discussing a special F-16 variant for Ukraine, with a modern AESA radar, longer range, and a wider choice of weapons, though no firm deal exists yet.
Ukraine is also counting on Swedish Gripen fighters. Ihnat says Ukrainian pilots are drawn to them for their lower operating costs and simpler maintenance, with the country likely to receive older C/D models first, before the newer Gripen E that Saab is developing.
Ukrainian pilots have already begun their training on the Gripen, a jet seen as a counter to the Russian aircraft dropping guided glide bombs on the front, though delivery timing depends on further agreements.

articles.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
articles.body:
The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”
Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.
The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.
Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.
“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.
When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”
US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.
Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.
US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.
Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.
His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.
Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.
Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.
Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”
Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.
Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.
Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.
Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.
Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.
Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

articles.title: Germany’s elite special forces unit is preparing for a possible war with Russia - media
articles.body:
Germany’s elite special forces unit is preparing for a possible war with Russia - media
Kyiv • UNN
Germany’s KSK special forces unit has changed its training due to a possible conflict with Russia. The soldiers are training to operate against tanks, artillery and drones.
The German Special Operations Command (KSK) is reviewing its training program in light of a possible military conflict with Moscow. BILD reports, according to UNN.
Details
"We are very specifically orienting ourselves toward an adversary represented by Russia," KSK commander Andreas Kühne said in an interview with BILD.
According to him, operations used to be planned for approximately three days, but now the soldiers are preparing to remain in the field for much longer. In addition, the special forces are once again training to face an adversary equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare capabilities. They are also practicing operations in extreme cold: the KSK is preparing for conditions typical of the eastern flank.
The unit is based at the Zeppelin Barracks in Calw, near Stuttgart. Approximately 1,500 personnel serve in the KSK. However, only one-third of them are special forces operators; the rest are administrative staff. The selection process is extremely rigorous: only about 15% of candidates pass it.
Just a few years ago, the future of the most elite unit hung by a thread. Incidents involving far-right extremists, a Nazi salute and pig heads at a farewell party, missing ammunition, and the discovery of a weapons and explosives cache at a KSK soldier's home shook the unit. In 2020, one of the special forces unit's companies was disbanded.
We remind you
The President of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Martin Jäger, considers the threat of an armed confrontation between Germany and Russia to be real.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter jet to get hypersonic missile
articles.body:
- Castelion received a contract modification from the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin integrating its Blackbeard hypersonic missile onto the F-16.
- The company did not disclose the value or timeline, and the U.S. Navy has already ordered 444 Blackbeard missiles for production.
Hypersonic missile startup Castelion has received a contract modification from the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin integrating its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon onto the F-16 fighter jet, the company announced on Oct. 26, bringing the missile one step closer to the U.S. Air Force after earlier work for the U.S. Navy and U.S. Army.
Castelion did not disclose the value of the modification, how long the integration work will take, or when the first test launch from an F-16 could happen, and the U.S. Air Force has not commented on the award.
“Castelion has been awarded a contract modification to its existing work with the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin Blackbeard integration activities with the F-16. We are grateful to the Air Force for their trust,” the company wrote on X.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering inside the atmosphere, which makes it harder to intercept than a ballistic missile on a predictable arc, and Castelion has built the program around producing it cheaply and in large numbers. The company, founded in 2022 by former SpaceX engineers and based in Torrance, California, is building a factory campus in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, aimed at turning out 500 weapons a year.
The Air Force Research Laboratory added $16.4 million to an existing Castelion contract in September, raising its total value to $37.2 million, for work on a low-cost, mass-producible long-range strike weapon running through June 2028. Castelion described the F-16 award as a modification to its existing work with the laboratory, though it did not say whether it falls under that same contract.
The U.S. Navy is furthest along with the weapon. It awarded $105 million in April to integrate Blackbeard onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and carry out live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific, ordered 50 early operational capability weapons in June, and in August awarded nearly $90 million to move Blackbeard toward a formal program of record, including features meant to speed sales to allies. In September, the Navy placed a first production order worth up to $200 million for 444 missiles. The U.S. Army received an integration award in October 2025 for a ground-launched version compatible with the HIMARS rocket launcher.
Putting Blackbeard on the F-16 would give it a launch platform far more common than the Super Hornet. The F-16 remains the most numerous fighter in the U.S. Air Force and flies with more than two dozen other countries, although Castelion has not said whether the integration work covers export versions of the jet.

articles.title: Israeli media highlights Egypt’s Rafale deployment as part of broader regional deterrence strategy
articles.body:
Israeli media have highlighted the deployment of Egyptian Rafale fighter jets on the eastern front, describing the move as part of a broader military strategy aimed at strengthening Egypt’s deterrence capabilities and maintaining operational readiness across multiple regional fronts.
The Israeli platform Ntziv.net reported that Egypt possesses an advanced network of modern airbases, challenging the assumption that its most sophisticated fighter aircraft are positioned toward Israel because of insufficient infrastructure elsewhere in the country.
According to the platform, Egypt’s deployment of modern combat aircraft, particularly the French-made Dassault Rafale, reflects a strategy of multi-front deterrence, strategic independence and regional power projection extending beyond its eastern border.
The report identified Gabal al-Basur Air Base, northwest of Cairo, as the principal operating base for Egypt’s Rafale fleet, noting that it is located well inside Egyptian territory, away from the Sinai Peninsula and the Israeli border.
It emphasised that the Rafale is a multirole fighter aircraft with an operational radius of approximately 2,000 kilometres, allowing it to conduct missions across several strategically important areas without requiring permanent deployment at forward bases.
These areas include Libya to the west, the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea and the Sinai Peninsula.
The platform also pointed to Egypt’s extensive network of operational airbases, including facilities in Mersa Matruh and Sidi Barrani near the Libyan border, as well as Aswan in southern Egypt.
It noted that Cairo has invested billions of dollars in modernizing its air force infrastructure, including the development of Berenice Airbase on the Red Sea coast, a strategic facility designed to accommodate advanced combat aircraft.
The report argued that Egypt’s air force modernization should not be viewed exclusively through the lens of its military relationship with Israel, but rather as part of a wider doctrine of active deterrence and strategic autonomy.
It further suggested that Egypt has sought to diversify its military suppliers to reduce dependence on the United States, particularly given Washington’s restrictions on certain advanced weapons exports intended to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge.
According to the Israeli platform, Egypt’s acquisition of Rafale fighters from France has enabled Cairo to obtain advanced radar and missile capabilities outside the framework of US arms export restrictions.
The report concluded that Egypt’s Rafale fleet and expanding military infrastructure reflect a broader effort to maintain operational flexibility across several regional theaters while strengthening the country’s independent defense capabilities.

articles.title: Six injured in Russian strikes on Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia, Chernihiv, officials say
articles.body:
Oct 26 (Reuters) - A Russian strike on Ukraine’s southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured four people overnight, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram on Monday.
Two more were injured in Russian strikes on the Chernihiv region, Ukraine’s emergency service said on the messaging app.
Also on Telegram, the Russian defence ministry said it hit a power station in Ukraine’s second largest city of Kharkiv, a warehouse in the surrounding region and another power station in the Khmelnitskiy region.
In addition, it targeted port infrastructure in Chornomorsk and a cargo vessel en route to Odesa used for military purposes, the ministry said.
The United States has pressed Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, which it argues added to high energy prices, a sensitive issue for the Trump administration amid its war on Iran as midterm elections approach next month.
In an interview aired on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said that in order for Kyiv to halt the strikes, Moscow must stop hitting power infrastructure.
Alternatively the United States should allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect missile launch sites, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles, he added.
(Reporting by Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo; Editing by Tom Hogue)

articles.title: Lithuania Deploys Army to Guard Border, Officially Targeting Russian Deserters
articles.body:
Lithuanian Armed Forces units have been deployed to patrol the border town of Vištytis, near Russia’s Kaliningrad region, amid the threat of Russian deserters illegally crossing the border.
BNS reported this, citing the Lithuanian State Border Guard Service.
The deployment of around 100 troops for patrol duties will continue until mid-November as a preventive measure amid the possibility of a new mobilization wave in Russia.
Amid the threat of escapees from Russia crossing the border, monitoring has been stepped up across all sectors — on land, on water, and in the air.
The deployment of military personnel has nearly doubled patrol coverage along the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region. This section is approximately 300 km long.
In the Vištytis area, the border runs through a lake, marked by special buoys. Video surveillance systems and patrol boats monitor the waters.
Lithuanian border guards are preparing for possible illegal crossings from Russia, as two Russian citizens entered the country via the frozen lake earlier this year.
Personnel from the National Defense Volunteer Forces have been on patrol duty. They serve at four border posts, rotating every 4–5 days.
The joint mission lets military personnel learn the specifics of border protection and prepare to take up defensive positions if the situation escalates.
The military presence at the border does not disrupt daily life in the town, and the heightened inspection regime follows standard state border-protection procedures.

articles.title: Serbia will not impose Russia sanctions – election winner’s rep to RT
articles.body:
Serbia will not impose Russia sanctions – election winner’s rep to RT
Serbia will maintain its longstanding ties with Russia and will not impose sanctions on Moscow despite EU pressure, a representative of the winning Student List movement has told RT Balkan.
The student-led opposition secured 52.73% of the vote in Sunday’s parliamentary election, according to the latest preliminary results, defeating the coalition of former President Aleksandar Vucic. He conceded defeat but warned that Belgrade could abandon its resistance to EU pressure and sanction Russia within months.
The movement emerged from nearly two years of anti-government protests sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people.
Speaking on Monday, Jovo Bakic, a university professor and Student List representative, said: “We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector.”
“There will be no changes in that regard,” he added.
Recalling the harsh UN sanctions against Yugoslavia in the 1990s, when Serbia was one of its constituent republics, Bakic said restrictions imposed by “small Serbia” would have little effect on Russia but would be “symbolically very bad” for Belgrade.
🇷🇸 Jovo Bakić za RT Balkan: Studentska lista neće uvoditi sankcije Rusiji ▪️Predstavnik "Studentske liste", profesor Jovo Bakić ponovio je da nova vlada Srbije neće uvoditi sankcije Rusiji, uprkos tvrdnjama bivšeg predsednika Aleksandra Vučića da će se to dogoditi za nekoliko meseci. "Mi Rusiju poštujemo i kao veliku silu i kao našu istorijski važnu partnerku i u mnogim slučajevima zaštitnicu. Tu (u spoljnoj politici zemlje) neće biti nikakvih promena", izjavio je Bakić gostujući u emisiji "Srbija bira" na TV RT Balkan.
— RT Balkan (@rtbalkan) October 26, 2026
Under Vucic, Serbia resisted EU demands to adopt the bloc’s restrictions on Russia over the Ukraine conflict, despite pursuing EU membership. The Student List campaigned primarily on domestic reforms, leaving several contentious foreign policy questions unaddressed.
According to Reuters, leading candidates of the victorious movement have said the incoming government would halt arms exports to conflict zones, including sales to Western intermediaries that subsequently supply weapons to Ukraine.
Vucic previously said European buyers could decide how to use Serbian ammunition, including whether to send it to Ukraine, although Belgrade has denied supplying Kiev directly.
Energy ties present another major issue for Serbia’s incoming government. Russia remains the country’s dominant gas supplier, accounting for roughly three-quarters of its needs. In March, Vucic said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to maintain deliveries on favorable terms, at prices far below those in most of Europe. The agreement was subsequently prolonged through the end of 2026.
Serbia also faces uncertainty over its oil supplies due to US sanctions on NIS, the majority Russian-owned energy company that runs the country’s only oil refinery. Hungarian energy group MOL is seeking to acquire the Russian stake, while the current US waiver allowing NIS to continue business expires on October 30. The company has requested another extension to avoid disruptions to fuel supplies.
Unlike Serbia, the EU has sought to phase out Russian fossil fuel imports and secure alternative suppliers since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Asked about pressure to abandon Russian energy supplies, Bakic said: “We are not here to satisfy foreigners, but to act in our national interest.”
The Kremlin said on Monday that it hoped to maintain mutually beneficial relations with Serbia. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic’s contribution to bilateral ties and added “As you know, it takes two to tango.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy welcomes Student List’s win in Serbia and says Kyiv is “ready to keep increasing cooperation”
articles.body:
For 14 years, Serbia’s government kept the country close to Moscow. Now, the opposition “Student List” has won the country’s snap parliamentary election, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine is ready to deepen its cooperation with Serbia, welcoming the result as “a new page” in a post on X.
The win could end the 14-year rule of President Aleksandar Vučić’s political force and weaken Moscow’s position in the Balkans. Serbia has remained an important Kremlin partner in Europe since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Belgrade never joined the EU's sanctions against Moscow.
“A new page”
In his post, written in Ukrainian, Zelenskyy said that "changes have taken place in Serbia, the victory of the Student List, and this is clearly a new page in the history of the country and its people."
“We wish Serbia success, real development, and warm relations with the European community,” he wrote.
He said Ukraine was grateful to Serbia “for the respect shown to our people and our state, our independence,” and added: “We are ready to keep increasing our cooperation, and may all the good hopes of the people of Serbia come true.”
But the winners rule out sanctions on Russia
Vučić had earlier predicted that a new government could impose restrictions on Moscow by March or April, according to Novosti. The Student List says otherwise: it has no plans to align with the EU or to sanction Russia over the war in Ukraine, according to Reuters.
Its candidates frame Serbia’s reliance on Russian gas, with Gazprom as the largest supplier at around 2.2 billion cubic meters a year at below-market prices, as an acute economic dependency rather than a geopolitical alignment.
The movement’s top candidates have also said a future government would end all arms exports to war zones, including sales to Western intermediaries who pass weapons to Ukraine. Around €800 million worth of Serbian ammunition has reached Ukraine through that route since 2022.

articles.title: Kazakhstan prepares a list for Moscow, Kenya appeals to Kyiv: three governments try to get citizens out of Russia’s war
articles.body:
Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Kenya are seeking the return of citizens drawn into Russia’s war, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) said on 25 October. According to relatives and officials the agency cites, many of the men had gone to Russia for work, only to be tricked or forced into its army.
Russia fills its ranks partly with foreigners. In April, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said the Russian Defense Ministry plans to enlist at least 18,500 of them in 2026. Foreign recruits let the Kremlin put off hard choices about another mobilization at home, the Atlantic Council argued in May. Home governments have pushed back before, among them Ghana in August. The new statements show the limit of that pushback. Once a man is serving in Russia’s army, his government has to ask Russia to let him go.
Kyrgyz minister: contracts are forced in enlistment offices and jails
Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev addressed the problem at a parliamentary committee on 13 October, answering lawmakers’ questions. He said Kyrgyz citizens in Russia are forced to sign contracts at military enlistment offices or in pretrial detention centers. If warned in time, diplomats try to stop the men from reaching the front.
Kazakhstan is compiling a list for Moscow
Kazakhstan is negotiating with Russia over citizens in the combat zone. Its Foreign Ministry said on 7 October that it was checking each hotline request. Once the checks are complete, the ministry said, it will send the compiled list to the Russian side.
SZRU separately cited unnamed relatives of one Kazakh worker. After he complained about working conditions, they said, he and other men were taken to an enlistment office and forced to sign contracts.
Kenya wants five men held by Ukraine treated as possible trafficking victims
Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, who also handles foreign affairs, gave lawmakers a count on 8 October. “The Ministry has records of 354 Kenyan nationals involved in the Russian-Ukraine crisis,” he told them. Families who petitioned Parliament dispute that number and put their own count at 841, Kenya’s The Star reported.
Kenya says Russia agreed to stop recruiting its citizens – families of the missing are still waiting
Ukraine holds five Kenyans captured while fighting for Russia, and Nairobi has already appealed to Kyiv over them. The government told Parliament it wants them treated as people who may have been trafficked abroad.
For Kenyans still serving in Russia’s army, the way out runs through Russian officers. Moscow informed Nairobi that unit commanders will consider requests to end military contracts case by case, the same government response said.

articles.title: Could Syria help Saudi Arabia fight the Houthis without troops?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria denied plans to send troops to Yemen – but how could it still help Saudi Arabia?
Reports have continued to circulate about a possible deployment of Syrian fighters to Yemen despite Damascus' denials.
But analysts who spoke to The New Arab said such a move was unlikely given Syria’s own domestic security challenges, and suggested that any military support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis could take other forms, without involving troops on Yemeni territory.
Citing unnamed Yemeni intelligence sources, Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported that Riyadh and Damascus had held talks on transferring up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to Yemen.
It said a Syrian military delegation had recently visited the Saudi capital and the kingdom’s southern regions to assess the proposed deployment.
According to the newspaper, Brigadier General Khaled Khattab, formerly leader of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and now commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army, spent four days in the southern Saudi regions of Asir and Najran, accompanied by Saudi officers. The delegation reportedly visited sites being prepared to receive Syrian fighters.
Meanwhile, Brigadier General Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army’s Third Corps and a former Hayat Tahrir al-Sham commander, was said to have met Saudi officers at the defence ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, benefits and their expected military role. Al-Akhbar said the delegation had finalised logistical preparations for the transfer.
The New Arab could not independently verify Al-Akhbar’s claims.
Could Syria support Riyadh without entering Yemen?
Muaz al-Abdallah, a Syria analyst at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), told The New Arab that any Syrian military support to Saudi Arabia would not necessarily involve deploying troops inside Yemen.
He said one possibility was that Syrian forces could be sent to help protect Saudi Arabia’s southern border, rather than take part directly in the fighting against the Houthis on Yemeni territory. Al-Abdallah said this statement left open the possibility of military cooperation with Riyadh, even if Damascus maintained that it had not deployed forces inside Yemen.
"Damascus has said it has not sent forces to Yemen, while also expressing support for Saudi security and saying military cooperation would take place through official channels and bilateral agreements," Al-Abdallah said.
He added that deploying Syrian personnel to the Saudi side of the border would not necessarily contradict the government’s denial that it had sent forces to Yemen, but could instead represent another way of supporting Riyadh.
Al-Abdallah suggested that Saudi Arabia could increase its financial assistance and investments in Syria’s reconstruction in return for military support.
Syrian drone expertise could help Saudi Arabia
Al-Abdallah also pointed to the potential for Syria to offer expertise in drone operations, particularly given its forces' experience operating drones during the war against Bashar Al-Assad’s regime. He said drones had played an important role in the lightning rebel offensive that toppled Assad, giving Syrian forces considerable experience in their use.
That expertise could prove useful to Saudi Arabia amid its confrontation with the Houthis, particularly if cooperation were to involve training or the use of smaller attack drones.
Al-Akhbar also reported that Syrian drone specialists were already involved in training forces in Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and that Syrian operators had helped establish drone units within Saudi emergency forces. However, these claims have not been independently verified.
Despite the reports, Al-Abdallah said ACLED had not documented evidence of Syrian fighters currently operating in Yemen. The organisation had found no reports of Syrian casualties, captured fighters or funerals linked to a deployment there, he said, noting that such evidence had helped establish the presence of Syrian fighters in other conflict zones, including Libya.
Al-Abdallah also questioned reports, including those published by Axios, that Syria could send its 84th Division to Yemen. He said the division was deployed around Suweida, in southern Syria, which remains largely outside the central government’s control after last year's sectarian clashes.
"Given the situation there, and reports of heavy Israeli arming of the National Guard and a possible escalation with the Syrian government, I don’t see how this division would leave Suweida," he said.
Syria's unresolved issues make deployment unlikely
The prospect of Syria deploying fighters to Yemen remains unlikely given the transitional government’s security challenges at home, according to Benjamin Schmida, a Middle East researcher at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Schmida told The New Arab that Saudi Arabia likely requested that Syria send forces to Yemen, but Damascus appears to have declined.
"It does not seem like these discussions proceeded very far beyond consulting CENTCOM," he said, adding that the Syrian government’s public rejection of the request suggested the talks had not continued.
Schmida said it remained unclear what forces Syria could realistically deploy, given the security challenges facing the country, including Kurdish areas in the northeast, Druze militia control over Suweida, sporadic Islamic State group attacks, and repeated Israeli incursions in the southwest.
He also cautioned against assuming that foreign fighters integrated into Syria’s military would be available for deployment abroad.
"Foreign fighters, such as Uyghur Turkistan Islamic Party fighters that are integrated into the Syrian Defence Ministry, represent some of Syria’s most elite units," he said.
"The Syrian government likely views integrated foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, as vital assets for Syria's defence and internal security that must remain in Syria in the event of a future crisis."
Would Syrian fighters change the balance in Yemen?
The possibility of transferring foreign fighters to Yemen was also raised in Al-Akhbar's report, which suggested that Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks, Afghans, and Chechens who joined Syrian opposition factions before Assad’s fall could be among those considered for deployment.
However, Schmida said the potential impact of any Syrian deployment would depend on the number of fighters sent and where they were integrated into the conflict.
Axios recently reported that Syria could send between 10,000 and 20,000 fighters. Schmida said this would represent a sizeable proportion of Syria’s total army manpower and could meaningfully bolster forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, whose forces he estimated at around 100,000.
But he noted that the Houthis are a much larger force, while government-aligned fighters remain spread across several frontlines, including Taiz, Marib, and Jawf.
More importantly, he said, sending additional fighters would not necessarily address the divisions undermining the Yemeni government’s war effort.
"Merely sending more fighters - though they may be experienced - is unlikely to solve one of the primary challenges for the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis: its own internal disunity," Schmida said.
He pointed to the political fragmentation and poor military coordination among government-aligned forces, warning that they could struggle to integrate Syrian fighters effectively, limiting their ability to change conditions on the battlefield.
Ultimately, Schmida said a meaningful Syrian deployment was unlikely "at this time or in the foreseeable future," as the government’s focus on domestic stability took precedence over Saudi requests.
While Riyadh could potentially use aid and investment to encourage Damascus to provide military support, he warned that doing so "could risk souring the Syrian-Saudi relationship and pushing Syria closer to Turkey or Saudi rivals like the UAE".
Louay Faour is a journalist at The New Arab focusing largely on the Levant, with a particular interest in Lebanese affairs
Follow him on X: @LouayFaour

articles.title: Koretsky: government must deliver new mobilization social contract by Dec 1
articles.body:
Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky predicts that following changes to the reservation system, over 90-95% of employees in the fuel-energy and defense-industrial complexes will be re-reserved.
"We are separating the concept of criticality from economic reservation criteria. This is very important. Why? Because salary and the absence of tax debt are not the same as an enterprise's criticality. This is important, it indeed brings transparency, cleanup, and additional revenues, but it does not equal criticality. Critical means energy, the defense-industrial complex, communications, housing and communal services, pharmacies, groceries, logistics, and so on. But there are enterprises, a large number already, that got there largely due to salaries and a lack of tax debts. Therefore, we are separating criticality from the economy," Koretsky said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) themed "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He emphasized that workers currently in the energy sector or the defense-industrial complex have nothing to worry about, as over 90-95% will be re-reserved.
"However, creating a large number of enterprises, whether IT or conditionally defense industry, where three drones are made and hundreds of people are reserved – I am conditionally simplifying, hyperbolizing in a certain sense, but that is how it is. And there are very many such cases. Contracting organizations. And it grows, grows, grows," he added.
According to the Prime Minister, changing the rules is designed, on the one hand, to cut down on unfair reservations without letting the economy collapse, and on the other hand, to give active military personnel a clear understanding regarding rotations.
"To say that these mobilization and reservation rules will produce a super-effect – no, there is no such thing, but we are at least stopping the endless growth of sometimes unfairly reserved individuals. And now, most importantly, what I am appealing to enterprises, business, and the economic sector about: we need to jointly come up with a new social model where, even if everyone is reserved, enterprises provide predictable mobilization of people into the army. This is an idealistic model. If such a solution could be found, the need to search for people on the streets would disappear. And if a business, entrepreneur, manager, or head takes on such a commitment – then nothing else is needed at all, this is a new social contract. But not thinking about it, not preparing for it, is a super-strategic mistake," Koretsky stated.
He stressed that failing to prepare in advance for a potential tightening of mobilization in Russia, which could reach 300,000–500,000 troops, would mean being forced to make unpopular decisions in manual mode once again.
"Then it won't be about reservations, or percentages. The issue is the survival of the state, and therefore this must be taken into account. Seeking to increase accountability for those who hide is also on the agenda – this is all a comprehensive story. By December 1, we must deliver a new social contract," he added, announcing a meeting with businesses on this issue.
As reported, on October 23, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky stated that the Cabinet of Ministers had finalized changes to the reservation system – an enterprise's criticality is being separated from its economic indicators, sectoral and regional criticality criteria will be updated, and enterprises will be checked for abuses.
The second change is that the maximum reservation level, particularly for the energy sector and defense industry, will no longer be 100% (dropping to 95%). The government will not weaken the work of those manufacturing weapons or maintaining critical infrastructure, and if uninterrupted operation requires reserving more, the enterprise can submit a justified appeal to a special Coordination Center.
The third change involves the Ministry of Defense strengthening liability for draft evasion. The fourth is the preparation of a mechanism for 100% reservation provided mobilization obligations are fulfilled: an enterprise will be able to fully reserve employees if it regularly and voluntarily recruits a portion of them for military service.
The Cabinet has also initiated a review of sectoral and regional criticality criteria, taking into account new requirements within 10 days.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: What is known about FSB’s thwarted attack on Moscow air defense site
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) detained two men from the South Caucasus who, acting on orders from the Ukrainian State Security Service (SBU), were preparing an attack using FPV drones against one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility, the FSB press office reported.
TASS has compiled the key information known at this time.
Thwarting of terrorist attack
- The FSB thwarted the sabotage and terrorist activities of two men from the South Caucasus, born in 1991 and 1998, the press office reported.
- According to the Federal Security Service, the men were going to prepare attack drones obtained from hidden stashes, transport them to the Moscow Region for launch, and activate them before takeoff.
- It was specified that the drones were to be controlled remotely from Ukrainian territory.
- While preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electric power facility and one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system, the suspects were detained by FSB officers, the press office said.
- The FSB released a video showing the FPV drones that the two detainees, natives of the South Caucasus, were using, on orders from the SBU, to prepare an attack on one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility.
- A video provided by the FSB press office shows the suspects assembling the drones and getting them ready for use according to instructions from their handler.
- The video shows two drones, both disassembled and assembled, as well as the communication devices used by the agents and instructions for assembling the drones.
Recruitment
- According to the FSB, one of the detainees was recruited by an SBU officer. Acting on his orders and in exchange for a promised monetary reward, the detainee traveled to Russia to plan a terrorist attack.
- To this end, he enlisted the help of a close acquaintance. Together, they retrieved FPV drones and components for homemade explosive devices from hiding places in the Smolensk and Kaluga Regions.
- The FSB had prior intelligence indicating that individuals from the South Caucasus were preparing an FPV drone attack on air defense and energy facilities in Moscow on behalf of the SBU. These individuals were agents of the Ukrainian special services, just like their handler, an FSB officer reported.
- The operation involving the handlers is ongoing, he noted.
Investigation
- A criminal case has been initiated against the detainees under Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code (Participation in a Terrorist Organization).
- The court remanded them into custody.

articles.title: Russia’s Sberbank links the crypto networks used by Moscow and Tehran to evade sanctions, Middle East Forum says
articles.body:
The U.S.-based think tank Middle East Forum has recommended that the U.S. Treasury Department treat cryptocurrency platforms used by Russia and Iran as a single interconnected system, according to a report published by the organization on Oct. 25. The report’s authors said Iran-linked Shelbit, Russia’s A7 network, and Kyrgyzstan-based crypto exchange TokenSpot all use shared infrastructure built around the USDT stablecoin, and that Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank, acts as the key link between the exchanges, as it “coordinates and legalizes” the final transactions.
The report outlined how Sberbank’s role expanded after Vladimir Putin signed Federal Law No. 282-FZ on Aug. 4, allowing Russian companies to settle foreign trade transactions using digital currencies. Kaplan Panesh, deputy chairman of the State Duma’s Budget Committee, said the law allows companies to pay foreign partners while “circumventing sanctions.”
Sberbank, which has been under full U.S. sanctions since 2022, began processing crypto payments of this kind immediately after Putin’s signature brought the law into effect. According to the report, that gave Russia access to state-backed payment channels operating in parallel with the A7 network.
Shelbit, which has companies in Georgia, Poland, and the United Arab Emirates, was sanctioned by the United States in August for transferring funds linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). TRM Labs estimates that $6.3 billion passed through Shelbit-linked wallets, including $318 million connected to A7. In September 2025, the platform transferred $2 million to a wallet that Israel later identified as being part of Hamas’ financial infrastructure. TRM Labs cautioned, however, that while blockchain data can show the path of funds, it does not establish what participants knew about the ultimate destination or purpose of the transactions.
TRM Labs also assessed that TokenSpot serves as a front for Grinex (the successor to the sanctioned Russian crypto exchange Garantex), and that it had transferred around $680 million to A7. The United Kingdom imposed sanctions on TokenSpot on Oct. 8. The United States has not yet done so, and as of Oct. 10, Kyrgyzstan’s financial regulator still listed the exchange as licensed.
The authors separately pointed to Putin’s August law allowing digital-currency settlements in foreign trade, after which Sberbank immediately began facilitating such payments.
The Middle East Forum recommended that the United States sanction TokenSpot and also proposed targeting Russian banks that process cryptocurrency payments for Iranian counterparties. Its authors suggested warning those banks that they could face the same treatment as VTB, which was sanctioned in September over its involvement in payment channels using rubles and Iranian rials.
The report also said the U.S. Treasury should seek to freeze USDT held in wallets linked to A7. According to a report by the Democratic minority in the U.S. Senate, 84% of 846 sanctioned crypto wallets linked to Iran used USDT.
On Oct. 1, the U.S. Treasury Department designated A7 as a transnational criminal organization, while the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) proposed cutting the network’s subagents off from the U.S. financial system.
According to the Treasury Department, more than $17 billion passed through those intermediaries between January 2025 and June 2026. The network was used by Iran’s central bank, the IRGC, and Hamas.
A7 was created in late 2024 by Russia’s Promsvyazbank and fugitive Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor.

articles.title: Palestine, Iran, world leaders welcome Lula Brazil election win
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Palestine, Iran and world leaders celebrate Brazil's Lula election win
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian have joined world leaders in congratulating Brazil's Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his historic re-election, with Abbas praising the Brazilian leader's support for Palestinian rights and Tehran calling for closer bilateral ties.
The messages came on Monday after Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday's presidential run-off, securing a fourth, non-consecutive term with 51.76% of the vote against his rival's 48.24%.
In a congratulatory telegram, Abbas praised Brazil's longstanding support for the Palestinian people and their national rights, as well as its condemnation of crimes committed against Palestinians.
He expressed appreciation for Brazil's solidarity with Palestine and confidence that Lula would maintain these positions during his new term.
Abbas also described the election result as a reflection of the Brazilian people's confidence in Lula's domestic and international policies, praising what he called the president's courageous and responsible positions.
Brazil has emerged under Lula as an important international voice in support of Palestinian rights, with his re-election expected to ensure continuity in the country's foreign policy towards the Middle East.
Iran calls for stronger ties and multilateral cooperation
Iranian President Pezeshkian also congratulated Lula, expressing hope that relations between Tehran and Brasilia would expand during the Brazilian leader's new term.
According to Iran's IRNA news agency, Pezeshkian called for greater cooperation in areas of mutual interest and efforts to strengthen multilateralism and international peace.
Iran and Brazil maintain friendly diplomatic relations and are both members of BRICS, the grouping of emerging economies that has sought to strengthen cooperation among countries outside traditional Western-led institutions.
The congratulations follow diplomatic contacts between the two countries, including a telephone conversation between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Brazilian counterpart Mauro Vieira on 19 October, ahead of the presidential run-off.
Lula's victory is also expected to reinforce Brazil's role in the Global South and its engagement with international organisations such as BRICS, at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions and strained relations with Washington.
China and Russia hail Lula's re-election
China and Russia were among the major international powers to welcome Lula's victory, highlighting Brazil's growing importance in international diplomacy.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun congratulated the Brazilian president and said Beijing was ready to continue developing its relationship with Brasilia.
China hoped to advance the two countries' shared strategic vision and strengthen cooperation during Lula's new term, he said.
The Kremlin also welcomed the result, with spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praising Lula's contribution to relations between Russia and Brazil and his role in developing BRICS.
Peskov expressed hope that Lula would continue pursuing closer cooperation with Moscow and other members of the grouping.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Lula, describing the result as a victory for democracy and multilateralism.
She pledged to continue working with Brazil on trade, climate action and the international rules-based order.
French President Emmanuel Macron called for stronger strategic cooperation between Paris and Brasilia, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed Lula's victory as part of what he described as a broader progressive resurgence.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also celebrated the result, declaring that democracy and the Brazilian people had prevailed.
Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel praised Lula's victory as a continuation of policies centred on sovereignty, peace and social justice.
Leaders from Canada, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Panama, Paraguay, Uruguay and Ecuador were also among those to congratulate the Brazilian president.
Divided reactions in the United States
The election prompted contrasting reactions from political figures in the United States, where relations with Brazil have been strained.
Donald Trump Jr, the son of US President Donald Trump, criticised the decision to extend voting hours by two hours during Sunday's run-off, accusing the American mainstream media of applying double standards in its coverage of the controversy.
The extension had been ordered by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin following procedural irregularities that disrupted the transportation of voters to polling stations in several Brazilian states.
Both candidates had requested additional voting time, but Bolsonaro subsequently called for the election to be annulled, describing the extension as unacceptable.
Progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders, meanwhile, congratulated Lula on his re-election, praising his record on workers' rights and democracy.
Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna welcomed the result as a rejection of extremism and urged Trump to respect Brazil's election outcome.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also celebrated Lula's victory, while California Governor Gavin Newsom's office welcomed continued cooperation with Brazil on democratic institutions, environmental protection and workers' rights.

Putin’s Valdai Residence Now Has 50+ Air Defense Positions—Half as Many as All of Moscow
Russia has built another 16 air-defense towers around Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s Valdai residence, bringing the number of identified air-defense positions in the surrounding area to more than 50, according to a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) investigation published October 25.
The new sites were identified through satellite imagery analyzed jointly with OSINT researcher jembob.

Investigators found that the 16 towers were constructed in October within roughly 50 kilometers south of the residence—the direction facing Ukraine.
The new structures appear to form an additional outer air-defense ring and are expected to host Pantsir gun-and-missile systems, Tor surface-to-air missile systems, or similar equipment.
No corresponding new positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the outer ring, although investigators said additional construction could follow.
The new defensive belt passes through Khotilovo military airfield and the area around the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
Khotilovo is used for Putin’s travel, and a dedicated railway line connects the airfield area with his Valdai residence. One air-defense tower at the base had already been constructed by March 2026.
Several additional positions have appeared around the reservoir, including near Lisiy Island. Russian forces have built a laboratory complex there that, according to an earlier RFE/RL investigation, may be connected to Russia’s biological weapons research program.
Construction of two air-defense towers near that facility began in early September, roughly when the investigation into the laboratory became public.
The latest expansion pushes the number of known air-defense positions around Valdai above 50.
That figure is particularly striking when compared with Moscow. Russia has built roughly twice as many air-defense positions to protect Moscow and the surrounding region since the beginning of the full-scale invasion—but Moscow and its suburbs are home to more than 20 million people.
Fewer than 100,000 people live in Valdai, the surrounding district, and nearby territory within roughly 50 kilometers.

articles.title: Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
articles.body:
Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous waters for commercial shipping, the Financial Times reported. At least 40 sailors have died there since the start of 2026, compared with 24 who died in the Strait of Hormuz, where the war the United States and Israel are waging against Iran has complicated shipping.
More than 570 ships have come under attack in the Black Sea since the start of the year, according to the maritime security firm Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization. Some ships were hit by accident, while others were deliberately targeted. Both Russia and Ukraine try to disrupt each other’s maritime shipping to reduce export revenues.
War-risk insurance for the Black Sea now costs as much as 15% of a ship’s hull value, almost twice the rate for ships in the Persian Gulf. Nearly the entire Black Sea is now classified in the highest war-risk category, except for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey.
Shipping oil from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz is now cheaper and safer by comparison. As a result, shipping companies increasingly refuse to operate in the Black Sea or use older vessels that are cheaper to insure.
Crews are recruited from Syria, Egypt, and Azerbaijan. The FT found that Syrian sailors earn about $800 a month working in the Black Sea. They are promised double pay for each day spent in the combat zone, and their families are to receive $25,000 to $50,000 in compensation if a sailor is killed.
Ukrainian forces struck more than 300 Russian vessels over an 11-week period, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said in September. The targets included sanctioned tankers as well as cargo ships carrying grain.
Russia has responded by stepping up strikes on ships entering Ukrainian ports. Russian attacks accounted for about 90% of strikes on commercial vessels over the past 45 days, according to Ambrey’s estimates.
The strikes are affecting global fuel and food supplies. Russian wheat exports fell 52% in September compared with a year earlier, while Ukraine is exporting only half its projected volume of agricultural products. Russian diesel exports fell by 467,000 barrels a day in September compared with a year earlier, according to Kpler.
The global effects of the war in the Black Sea are difficult to separate from those of the conflict in the Persian Gulf, Bloomberg reported. High global wheat stocks have kept disruptions in grain supplies from significantly affecting prices, while diesel fuel grew more expensive even before Russian–Ukrainian attacks escalated, because of the war the United States is waging against Iran.
The war in photographs
A family from Oleshky starts a new life in the Kyiv region
Vitaliy and Iryna fled the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in September with their 13-year-old son, Vlad, and their cat, Marsik. By then, residents had been left in complete isolation, without food, water, electricity, or medical care.
A drone damaged Vitaliy and Iryna’s home, prompting them to leave Oleshky and walk more than 20 kilometers (12 miles) along a mined road. The family traveled through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory and is now rebuilding its life in the Kyiv region.
Russia and Ukraine agreed last week to a ceasefire in Oleshky for the evacuation of residents. It is set to take effect at 4 a.m. on October 27.

articles.title: AFRL Moves Cargo Through Space with SpaceX Demonstration
articles.body:
Editor’s Note: This story was updated Oct. 26 with additional information from the Air Force Research Laboratory.
When a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket took off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Fla., on Oct. 20, it didn’t only carry the usual mix of micro-satellites and cubesats built by a wide range of companies. Also catching a ride into orbit was a capsule containing, among other things, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear, and emergency medical equipment.
That capsule wasn’t bound for the only humans in space on the International Space Station; it was a test of a capability that could one day get critical supplies to U.S. forces around the globe.
The Air Force Research Laboratory launched its Rocket Cargo initiative in 2021 to explore the idea of moving large amounts of cargo through space, a process that would both be faster and allow the Pentagon to more easily reach remote or contested areas.
SpaceX, which has demonstrated the ability to return its rockets to Earth and safely land them, was the first company to get a contract under the program in 2022, when AFRL awarded the firm a five-year, $102 million contract.
Other companies, including Blue Origin, Sierra Space, and Rocket Lab, have since signed on as well, but AFRL never announced any experiments or tests for the project—until now.
In a release, AFRL said the Oct. 20 mission “used a SpaceX capsule with instrumentation to measure temperature, shock and vibration; it carried agile cargo pod designs built for various delivery loads.”
The lab did not specify how many pods or how much equipment were included in the test and did not immediately respond to a query. But in a subsequent social media post Oct. 26, the lab said it recovered the pods after they splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. Each pod had equipment and sensors to monitor the payload’s status as it launched and then reentered the atmosphere.
“Researchers paid special attention to the electronics equipment, including a satellite communication-enabled tracker, batteries, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear and emergency medical equipment,” the release states.
The SpaceX capsule used in the test is called Starfall. Back in May, the Federal Aviation Administration released an environmental assessment for Starfall operations in the Pacific Ocean, describing it as a “cylindrical shaped capsule” with these dimensions:
- Approximately 0.75 meters (2.5 feet) tall
- A diameter of 3.1 meters (10.2 feet)
- A weight of 2,100 kilograms (4,600 pounds)
- Capable of carrying 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) of payload
- Total weight of 3,100 kilograms (6,800 pounds)
In June, SpaceX launched what it called a “Starfall Demo Mission,” ending with the capsule splashing down into the Pacific.
In a statement, AFRL’s Technology Transition Office director Adam Remaly touted the most recent test as a success.
“This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the future force,” Remaly said. “The cross-discipline collaborations and ability to unleash the speed of our defense industrial base are key to maximizing capability and winning the future.”
AFRL’s release noted that engineers also “measured the capsule to potentially include a life raft in future tests” on Oct. 20.
Rocket Cargo could one day deliver supplies “to contested environments and austere sites without access to runways and roads, including contested logistics, expeditionary operations, rescue operations, disaster relief and response to chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear hazards,” the release states.

articles.title: European defense ministers warn Putin isn’t looking for peace
articles.body:
Andrius Kubilius and Kaja Kallas attend a meeting of the E5, a five-country European defence and security cooperation group, at the French Defence Ministry in Paris, on October 26, 2026. | Thomas Samson/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Top European defense ministers and EU representatives said Ukraine faces challenging months ahead, insisting they must keep supporting Kyiv despite the U.S. bid for talks with Russia.
"The new diplomatic push is there, but it's also clear that Putin's actions tell a different story," the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a press conference in Paris on Monday. Kallas said she was expecting a "brutal winter" for Kyiv and that there was "no hope for imminent peace," reiterating the need to help Ukraine "withstand the attacks and increase the cost for Russia."
Kallas, along with European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, joined a meeting with defense ministers from the E5 group made up of France, the U.K., Germany, Poland and Italy, hosted at the French armed forces ministry.
Advertisement
The meeting came amid a renewed U.S. effort to push Ukraine into peace talks with Russia and growing doubts about Washington's support for Kyiv.
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said last week he would offer Russia's Vladimir Putin direct talks with President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to secure a ceasefire.
"No results whatsoever comes for those who want to negotiate with Putin," German defense minister Boris Pistoripus said. "The results are what? It doesn't lead to anything. There is no signal whatsoever that Putin is looking for peace."
The U.K.'s Wes Streeting added: "While none of us seek confrontation with Russia ... We do have to be aware of the threat posed by Russia."
While pledging "total transparency" with the U.S., France's Catherine Vautrin said the E5 members would "work together concretely," focusing on arms production and interoperability.
"Produce more, produce faster, produce equipment suited to today’s conflicts – but we must already be planning for the conflicts of tomorrow," Vautrin said. "On that, EU financial initiatives can help us move in this direction."

articles.title: Algeria to Deploy Troops Abroad for First Time Since 1973, Sending Forces to Niger
articles.body:
Algeria’s two parliamentary chambers approved on October 25 the deployment of the country’s armed forces to Niger to protect Algeria’s energy interests and honor bilateral agreements.
Algeria’s Council of the Nation, the upper house of parliament, made the announcement.
The decision was approved in closed-door sessions after President Abdelmadjid Tebboune submitted a request on October 22.
The lower house of parliament, the National People’s Assembly, also approved the troop deployment by an overwhelming majority.
According to an official statement by the Council of the Nation, the decision aims to protect Algeria’s energy interests and fulfill the terms of a bilateral agreement with Niger.
Algerian authorities have not yet disclosed the size of the military contingent, the exact deployment date, or the duration of the planned mission.
According to Reuters, one possible deployment site for Algerian troops is the Madama area in northern Niger, near the border with Libya.
Algeria has significant economic interests in Niger, particularly in oil production and the development of transcontinental energy projects.
The state-owned company Sonatrach is developing the Kafra oil project in northern Niger. In August 2026, its subsidiary ENAFOR was preparing to drill the Kafra Sud-Est 1 exploration well, approximately 85 km from the Algerian border.
Algeria, Niger, and Nigeria are also pursuing the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline project, which aims to transport natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria.
In June 2026, Sonatrach announced the start of construction on the pipeline’s Algerian section.
In August, Militarnyi reported that Algeria had deployed four Su-30 fighter jets to Niger following an attempted military coup in the country’s capital, Niamey.

Ukraine, the US, the EU, and NATO plan to meet in Brussels this week to discuss security for Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Ukrainian TV. The meeting would follow last week’s talks in Oslo and a US envoy’s visit to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Guarantees are what would oblige Ukraine’s allies to act if Russia attacks again. The Paris Declaration laid plans for that commitment in January. A day later, Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg and said he had brought papers setting out possible paths to a settlement. He told Putin the Oslo talks had been productive. Kallas said the EU’s naval Operation Aspides was helping keep cargo and oil flowing through the Red Sea.
